Our analysis revealed that the most extreme events tend to converge at localized celestial positions, some of which are known targets, while others are novel. The majority of these events reside near high-energy sources, such as active galactic nuclei, supernovae remnant cores, and young star clusters, often aligned with their jet directions. This study presents a novel dynamic model called Temporal-Varying Poisson Autoregression (TVPAR) to accurately represent and forecast time-series data exhibiting significant changes over time, particularly in their underlying structural components. Unlike conventional models that assume data stability or abrupt changes, TVPAR captures the evolution of parameter relationships through a combination of statistical techniques and machine learning, utilizing long short-term memory neural networks to model dynamic coefficients. Experimental TVPAR results demonstrate performance enhancements over current models in various evaluation metrics. Additionally, TVPAR's capabilities are demonstrated through applications in genetics and finance. The code for this research is available at https://github.com/ashawkey/TVPAR.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that combines the benefits of neural networks and descriptor fields to facilitate efficient and robust manipulation tasks. We envision NDFs as part of a larger framework that includes an invariant network encoding objects into a 10D vector, a neural regression model that produces a 3D grid of descriptor values from this encoding, and two alternative versions of the grid network: one that generates a 3D grid of normalizing flows via a multi-scale architecture and another that generates a 3D grid of Gaussian means and standard deviations via a simple architecture. We demonstrate the effectiveness of NDFs on challenging manipulation tasks in simulated environments, demonstrating how descriptors can be used for contact detection, action selection, and continuous control. Additionally, we show that NDFs in conjunction with a simple policy can be trained on real robots for a picking task. We also analyze the impact of different NDF components on performance and provide a setup guide for replicating our results. We hope this work inspires further development of NDFs, incorporating external sensors and more complex tasks in controlled environments. Our code is available at https://github.com/vishal-1099/neural_descriptor_fields.

In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a particular optimization procedure for a given function can be trusted to locate the function's minimum. To achieve this, researchers often rely on the combinatorial nature of a related model, known as the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model, whose properties have been rigorously examined through mathematical techniques. Building on previous work by M. J. W. Bonney, R. L. Joyner, and D. Sherrington, as well as more current results by A. A. Block and A. M. Sutiainen, we have established a lower bound for the second derivative of the TAP free energy in the high-temperature regime, thereby demonstrating the local concavity of the TAP energy within this temperature range. Furthermore, we have investigated the properties of the set of solutions corresponding to the most significant edges in the parallax map, and found that its distribution conforms to the Sudakov-Fernique law, which is a generalization of the Brunn-Minkowski inequality. Additionally, we have established the local concavity of the TAP energy through a different approach, using a stochastic gradient descent algorithm and a variant of the Ampersand-Monroe-Perry large deviation principle, which provides a more precise characterization of the set of solutions exceeding the most significant edge in the parallax map. This characterization enables us to extend the Sudakov-Fernike law to the case of random edge weights, which is a significant generalization of its original form. This extension is a novel contribution of this paper. In addition to aerosols, some have investigated retrieving other atmospheric components, such as gas concentrations, fire severity, and biomass, in order to expand the utility of this technique. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct tasks: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We combine projection grouping and correspondence learning by constructing a unified framework, Demodulation-and-Correspondence Network (DCN). Projections derived from a basic two-stage pipeline are fed into DCN, which learns optimal modulators and discriminative correspondences between projections and the 3D object via an explicit correspondence learning objective. We further introduce DCN to the pipeline, and with multiple initial guesses, a robust pose estimation framework known as DeepHMap++ is created. Experimental evaluations show that DeepHMap++ outperforms existing baselines across multiple datasets. Code is publicly available at: this http URL.

Our research extends the concept of significant eigenvector utilization to multi-layer networks. In single-layer networks, an eigenvector centrality metric known as the "betweenness" is used to identify prominent nodes that occupy critical positions in the network's shortest paths. Our study adapts this concept for multi-layer networks by determining the most significant eigenvector utilization that maximizes the number of layers that include a particular node in their respective centrality distributions. Our results show that this approach is equivalent to calculating the sum of each node's significance across all layers. Consequently, this indicates that the traditional approach of comparing the distribution of eigenvector centrality across layers may not be effective and that a more suitable method could be comparing the sum of node significances across layers instead. Our work also explores correlations between eigenvector centrality and other network metrics, with notable connections found in multi-layer networks. Finally, our research demonstrates applications of this work, including a novel method for validating random network generation. Our methods are demonstrated using real data, including collaboration networks and brain connectivity datasets. Our available code can be used for reproducing our results and for further developing this work. Our study highlights the potential of our methods for exploring complex networks and provides a foundation for future research on the eigenvector centrality of multi-layer networks. This study investigates how spheres with a liquid surface layer interact and seal with solid surfaces at various speeds. Experiments were conducted where spheres with a layer of water or kerosene collided with flat surfaces of the same or different materials, and the resulting seal patterns were classified based on the speed of impact, surface properties, and liquid properties. Three speed regimes were identified: low speed, where complete sealing occurs; an intermediate speed, characterized by incomplete sealing and the formation of rings; and a high speed, marked by fragmented seals. The development of a 2D model that simulates how the liquid layer and solid surface interact was also explored, along with a focus on the intermediate speed regime. The model was used to analyze the effects of different parameters on seal patterns and demonstrated its capability to accurately predict seal behavior. However, it was unable to simulate the transition between the low and intermediate speed regimes, and further enhancements are required to improve its performance. The study's findings and the model's results are combined to provide a comprehensive understanding of how spheres with a layer of liquid interact and seal with solid surfaces at various speeds. The proposed model offers a useful tool for further analysis and can be used to inform the development of more complex multi-physics models. We investigate the possibility of a Type IIB gravity background exhibiting a globally symmetric configuration in a 10-dimensional spacetime. My research reveals that, contrary to previous conclusions, there are actually no globally symmetric gravity backgrounds in 10-dimensional spacetime, even when allowing for symmetries that aren't consistently applied across the entire universe. As a result, I show that all globally symmetric backgrounds inevitably give rise to non-trivial $\theta$-terms in the effective field theory, with $\theta$ terms arising from the intersection of membrane and five-brane charges. These results have significant implications for the behavior of open strings, influencing the vacuum energy, gravi-dilaton interaction, and a specific dimensionless ratio that characterizes the spacetime geometry. Consequently, the range of these ratios that are compatible with the theory is found to be expanded. Quantum states known as single-photon facilitated coherent states have interesting properties, being resistant to decoherence while facilitating the interaction with a classical channel, and requiring a single photon to initiate their generation. These states could be generated with the quantum-optical catalysis method using a beam splitter, where a cavity system acts as the catalyst, and they possess unique quantum attributes that make them exceptionally versatile. Specifically, in a scenario with lossy channels, these states can efficiently convert the generated photons into a coherent amplitude, even with low levels of cavity loss. Furthermore, by modulating the cavity loss, it is possible to influence the quantum state of the output field, offering a delicate balance between resisting decoherence and optimizing the conversion of photons to coherent amplitude. Additionally, these states demonstrate the interconnection between the distributed and the trapped cavity system, allowing for the recovery of the initial state by reclaiming the cavity system. This achieves a state that is not only coherent but also allows for the recovery of the initial conditions, a hallmark of quantum catalysis. The practical application of these states is reflected in their ability to generate a double-peaked distribution of the output field amplitude, offering promise for the development of highly precise spectral analysis tools. The possibility of recovering the initial state conditions also offers possibilities for developing closed quantum systems, and by extending the single-photon facilitated coherent states to include two-photon states, it becomes possible to create a statistical distribution that is bimodal and resistant to decoherence, and which can be distinguished from a Schrödinger cat state. The challenge of distinguishing these states from a Schrödinger cat state is reflected in the difficulty of identifying the number of photons within a quantum state, a problem that persists even when considering the most advanced detection technologies. We introduce a technique for creating polynomial models using linear regression as a foundation.  This approach, which we refer to as PROF (Regression to Polynomial by Integer Optimization and Validation with Errors), takes a linear regression model and generates a corresponding polynomial model via the use of integer programming.  We demonstrate that this approach results in a comprehensive ensemble of polynomial models that incorporate the insights derived from linear regression and incorporate bounds on the coefficients of these models.  Additionally, we demonstrate that this approach provides robustness to outliers by incorporating the number of allowable outliers as a parameter in the integer programming framework.  We further demonstrate that this approach results in a computationally expensive method of building polynomial models using only the input data, and propose a number of suggested modifications to this method for reducing its computational intensity.  We test and validate this technique on a number of different examples, including datasets generated randomly and real-world datasets consisting of process data for a reactor.  We compare the results obtained from this technique against the results obtained from other methods of building polynomial models via the use of multiple metrics, including the accuracy of the models, the computational intensity of the method, and the robustness of the models to outliers.  We also provide a number of suggested applications of this technique for building polynomial models, including the use of linear regression as a preliminary analysis for identifying the inputs and outputs of a system, the use of integer programming to select the most important terms in a polynomial model, and the use of this technique for building models in the presence of noise in the data.  We conclude by summarizing the main findings obtained from this research, and provide a number of suggestions for modifying this technique and general methods of building polynomial models, including the use of other types of regression models as a foundation for polynomial models, the use of search heuristics for solving the integer programming problems, and the use of validation techniques for evaluating the performance of polynomial models.  We also provide a number of references to other types of methods for building polynomial models, including the use of Bayesian approaches, the use of neural networks, and the use of genetic programming. A new framework called DDAUnet for abdominal CT image neoplasm segmentation has been proposed, incorporating spatial attention and dense attention techniques to prioritize focal regions and aggregate contextual information, respectively. By leveraging both local and global context, as well as attending to significant areas, this method enables the creation of a high-quality neoplasm mask by contrasting the learned normal tissue features with those in the image. Evaluations using a large esophageal neoplasm dataset showed that DDAUnet outperformed several baseline models, with the Dice coefficient revealing a score of 0.79 and the mean absolute error of 14 voxels in a comparison with air as the background. Furthermore, a simple approach was developed to differentiate neoplasm type by training a binary classifier using a small set of features derived from extraction and ensemble techniques, with results indicating high classification accuracy of 95% for differentiating esophageal neoplasms from normal tissue. Code-mixed language refers to text that combines elements from two or more languages, a common practice especially among multilingual societies where people switch between different languages for various purposes, including online interactions. As a result, code-mixed language presents a significant challenge for traditional monolingual AI models, leading to subpar performance when these models are applied to coded data without previous training. In this article, we explore the issues that MVLM models encounter when dealing with code-mixed data, the impact of language interference and the lack of labeled data, as well as possible strategies for these models to acquire linguistic knowledge from coded resources, including the integration of pretrained multilingual models, explicit feature engineering, and data generation methods. In the course of this discussion, we also examine code-mixed classification and extraction tasks. When dealing with coded data, another important consideration is the ethical issue of linguistic respect. In the final section, we discuss potential future research areas, including the study of multilingual syntax and the creation of high-quality labeled data. Human-generated descriptions serve a purpose beyond simple language models - they can be used to evaluate the accuracy of automatic image descriptions. Despite this potential, human descriptions derived from crowdsourcing platforms are often subject to inconsistencies and biases, affecting their utility. Additionally, utilizing these descriptions for evaluation entails significant costs, posing a barrier for frequent use. This paper discusses various sources of reference data, exploring both paid and free crowdsourcing options and describing our own experience with the Amazon Mechanical Turk, detailing best practices for obtaining precise and reliable data. We demonstrate how to effectively use human descriptions to assess the completeness and clarity of automatic image descriptions generated using the Flickr30k dataset. Our approach involves evaluating the accuracy of hidden layers used for description generation and our findings show that, with proper training and careful selection of human responders, human descriptions can accurately assess the completeness and clarity of automatic descriptions. We also explore the generalizability of our findings to other image description datasets. Our work concludes by identifying potential sources of biased data and suggesting future research directions such as evaluating the reliability of hidden layers and the effectiveness of different crowdsourcing platforms. We openly provide our code and data at the following link: https://github.com/ghrasoul/HumanReferenceEvaluation.

Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. To further understand and identify these materials, research utilizes computational methods to simulate and examine the material's electronic and phononic behavior. However, an unresolved issue remains concerning the Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure, as multiple variants exist and competing results have been obtained from theoretical studies. To address this, we evaluated all possible variants of the Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure and compared them to experimental data on phonons and dielectric constants, ultimately determining that the results best match the results for alpha-Ta$_2$O$_5$. This version of the material exhibits a collaborative interaction between local and regional modes in its phonon spectrum and demonstrates unique phonon anomalies and local distortions that could be relevant to its minimal reflectivity and dielectric behavior. Given its dielectric characteristics, researchers believe alpha-Ta$_2$O$_5$ has potential applications in extreme ultraviolet technology. To further understand this material, researchers used $4\times 4$ Monte Carlo simulations of dielectric behavior driven by phonon anomalies and local distortions caused by irregular oxide bond lengths and configurations. These simulations successfully replicated the results for alpha-Ta$_2$O$_5$ and could be adapted for other complex oxide materials. They also highlight the promise of combining experimental analysis of phonons and ab-initio simulations of dielectric behavior in theoretical research.

Social connectivity across diverse populations is essential in combating the spread of misinformation. This study examines the impact of geographic separation on the transmission of false information in social networks. Based on years of data from Reddit, our findings reveal that greater distance between individuals accelerates the rate at which false information is shared, while the size of the surrounding environment slows down this dissemination process. Specifically, our results show that false information spreads more quickly in more isolated areas by a factor of approximately 25%, and a 15% decrease in dissemination rate is observed in larger environments. These outcomes hold constant various variables, including user credibility and posting frequency. Furthermore, false information spreads more rapidly during times when individual connections are less stable, and more isolated communities are more susceptible to false information in the initial stages of its release. This study provides insights into the dynamics of false information transmission, as well as the implications of reducing population connectivity, all set against the backdrop of advancing technology that could lead to increased geographic separation and potentially greater ease with which false information can be shared. Lastly, this research's findings have utility for numerous applications, including but not limited to, military operations, community management, and information validation strategies. Humans naturally generate rich auditory feedback while interacting with their environment, which enhances learning and teaching for other people.  Despite the benefits, most robotics learning labs ignore this aspect as they are typically designed to model human-robot interaction using text-based descriptions.  To address this gap, we are collecting an audio dataset in a laboratory setting where humans demonstrate various robot control tasks to other humans.  Our primary objectives in sharing this dataset are two-fold: firstly, making the dataset available for developing listening-based evaluation methods, and secondly, providing a foundation for exploring methods that can automatically assess teaching content for effectiveness.  Our assessment approach involves creating a metric to predict how easily a concept can be grasped from an audio explanation of a manipulation task based on the learner's level of expertise.  We are exploring a simple machine learning-based model to achieve this, and our results show that it is possible to accurately predict learning difficulty with a high degree of accuracy.  We believe that further optimization of our model, along with the availability of more training data, have the potential to lead to a more sophisticated insight: a way to generate high-quality teaching content from low-quality previous knowledge.  We hope that our findings and the accompanying dataset will spur interest among the robotics research community and inspire novel approaches in robotics learning.  Specifically, we are proposing two particular research directions: evaluating teaching content and generating effective learning content from scratch.  In addition to these proposals, we are also contributing a method for estimating the ease of learning from the audio recordings of a single demonstration, which can be useful on its own.  In addition, we are providing a detailed analysis of our model along with a comparison to an alternative approach based on a statistically-based method.  We are also outlining a possible path forward that involves incorporating temporal aspects of the recordings along with a possible way to interpret the model's predictions in terms of the learning difficulty in terms of the percentage accuracy.  Finally, we are contributing our dataset, model, and method in the form of three separate supplementary files.  Each file is self-contained, and each contains all the information required to reproduce our results along with our dataset.  Each of the three files is available at the website https://yonghojo.github.io/robot-teaching-evaluation/.  We hope that our contributions will facilitate interest and new approaches in robotics learning, specifically in learning from demonstration and teaching.  We believe that evaluating teaching content and generating effective learning content from scratch are two particular research directions that have the potential to lead to a major breakthrough in robotics

A complex field theory is defined as a set of classical Euler-Arnold equations parametrized by a Lie algebra, potentially with extensions given by certain quadratic structures. We have established that any such system can be reinterpreted through conformal field theory principles. Specifically, a complex field theory is equivalent to a conformal field theory with a symmetric spin triple operator, potentially along with additional operators that commute with each other under the Lie algebra's action. This classification of complex systems using the Euler-Arnold equations provides a novel Lie algebra-based interpretation, and we have explored various examples, including the Allen-Cahn, Cahn-Hilliard, and Harper equations. Additionally, this framework enables us to identify conserved quantities and determine the conformal field theory's symmetry group. Notably, one-dimensional examples can be straightforwardly analyzed using this method, although in higher dimensions the equation's solvability remains unclear. Nevertheless, one-dimensional solutions can be directly computed, and we have found that the Allen-Cahn and Harper equations' compacton solutions are conserved by the Weyl algebra, whereas the Cahn-Hilliard equation's solutions are conserved by the abelian Lie algebra, and these conclusions are validated through explicit calculations. Moreover, this approach is applicable to a broad class of systems, including two-dimensional examples like the planar Euler equation and the Murray-Meissner equation, which govern superfluid film dynamics. These systems are known to have circular symmetry, which significantly simplifies their analysis using the Euler-Arnold equations framework. Conversational interfaces such as robots and voice-based systems like Amazon Alexa and Google Assistant are becoming increasingly popular, and as a result, testing these systems has become a critical need. Although many methods exist for verifying the accuracy of structured data processing systems, conversational interfaces, being unstructured by nature, are more difficult to test through automation. Currently, testing conversational interfaces largely relies on a manual approach, which can be time-consuming and error-prone. In this paper, we present a automated testing framework for conversational interfaces based on their definitions in the form of natural language. This framework incorporates various validation techniques to ensure that each test case is accurate, effective, and easy to create, in addition to a state tracker that simulates the system under test and provides detailed information about each test case execution. The testing system includes a command-language interface that allows users to execute tests, review previous test runs, and retrieve individual test-case execution results. The paper includes a demonstration of the framework's capabilities through a working example. The proposed testing system is suitable for use in professional development environments, and it is available for download. The source code of the system can be modified to suit the needs of individual developers. The system's capabilities extend to testing conversational interfaces that generate natural language through machine learning, although currently such systems are considered difficult to test due to the lack of available documentation about their workings. The paper includes a discussion about the challenges of testing such systems and presents an approach for tackling these challenges. The approach involves creating partial test cases that can be used to validate the working of individual components of the system, and it also provides a standard definition for some common natural language elements called regular utterances. The paper concludes by highlighting the opportunities for further improvement and presenting some related work on testing conversational interfaces. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target scenarios are common paradigms used in cross-domain recommendation. In the single-target setting, recommendations are made for one user with sparse information, utilizing data from other users with more information. In the dual-target setting, recommendations are made for multiple users with sparse information, utilizing data from users with more information. Although both scenarios have been extensively explored, research on the dual-target setting is less common due to its greater difficulty. In this work, a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSDCR) is proposed to address the dual-target setting. Within this framework, multiple domains are treated as individual sources of truth, and a comprehensive attribute preference learning model is developed to manage and combine domain information. Ultimately, the SDKR score is used to make recommendations in the sparse domains. Experimental evaluations using real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of the MSDCR framework across multiple metrics. The proposed SDKR score provides a new reference point for evaluating and ranking users in the sparse domains. The code for this model is available at: https://github.com/zhou-yu/MSDCR.

Conic programs are effective for solving a broad range of optimization problems, and their potential is significantly enhanced when utilized within a two-step resolution process. However, natural conic expressions can hinder the performance of conic solvers by causing them to operate on non-convex problems, and identifying these expressions on large-scale models can be very challenging. This paper introduces a new tool, Hypatia, that is designed to automatically identify natural conic expressions within a model's variables and general conic representations, allowing conic solvers to bypass them in the resolution process. We present Hypatia's capabilities and demonstrate its impact on a set of large-scale models, showing that its capability to handle two-factor conic representations enables significant improvements in performance, and the ease of its integration into existing workflows makes it a valuable addition to our toolkit. We also explore the challenge of identifying natural conic expressions on variables that are defined as expressions, and provide a simple yet effective solution based on the expansion of these variables. Furthermore, we contribute a new feature to Hypatia that enables the automatic expansion of these variables, and analyze the impact of this expansion on the performance of a conic solver, using a new benchmark composed of models featuring complex variables. We intend for Hypatia to be a starting point rather than a comprehensive solution, and welcome any feedback that could further enhance its capabilities and our understanding of natural conic expressions and their resolution. We have openly sourced Hypatia's code and validation tests on GitHub, and believe that its utility extends beyond Julia, making it possible for users of other languages, such as Python and MATLAB, to replicate its functionality. We also discuss various strategies for resolving variables that are defined as expressions, and provide a comparative analysis of these methods on a range of small-scale test models. We conclude by outlining potential future extensions to Hypatia, such as the development of a feature detection system and the integration of different resolution strategies. The underlying mechanism of numerous complex systems can be represented by internal meetings among various agents. These interactions often result in meaningful actions that align with the system's objectives, although they are frequently inefficient and lack a clear sense of unity. To address this challenge, researchers have turned to multi-agent meeting models that prioritize incentive-based interactions among agents, offering a more precise and more predictive approach. In response to these advancements, this paper takes an innovative path by introducing a new model that excels in capturing the intricate patterns inherent to dynamic systems over time, as well as the problematic nature of their internal meetings. Unlike static models that fail to capture temporal nuances, the proposed approach uses reinforcement learning combined with incentive-based interactions among agents in recurring meetings, effectively distilling the systems' internal dynamics into actionable insights. To validate the effectiveness of this model, it has been applied to a broad range of complex systems across finance, ecology, and sociology, demonstrating its broad applicability and highlighting the mutual benefits that arise from healthy internal meetings among these systems. The resulting model and its underlying theory also offer valuable insights for system designers, indicating how to construct complex systems that are resilient, efficient, and aligned with their underlying purposes. The code for this model is available at https://github.com/thuylm/Recurrent-Meeting.

Coxeter groups stemming from buildings of type B possess distinctive root systems characterized by hyperplanes dividing space. These root systems can be further divided into A-type and B-type roots. In 1966, Coxeter established a significant result indicating that a change of basis occurs when a reflection operator is expressed in terms of other operators, with the number of basis changes equivalent to the number of A-type roots between the initial and final spaces. This process is referred to as'simplex transformation'. Previously unpublished work by L. H. Clark reveals that a simplex transformation can be perceived as a permutation of the defining coordinates, with the number of such permutations matching the number of B-type roots. Additionally, this number can be determined as the number of elements within the quotient of the group by its maximal abelian subgroup, following a generalization of Weyl's criterion. This generalization dictates that a root is elementary if and only if its corresponding reflection operator commutes with all other operators. Consequently, a root system is regarded as irreducible if it contains at least one non-elementary root. This study demonstrates that the aforementioned Coxeter result holds in the broader context of complex space, with (non-orientable) projective spaces equivalent to the original space following a simplex transformation. Furthermore, this study clarifies the relationship between the group's actions on the space and the root system, with the orientation-preserving subgroups corresponding to the B-type roots and the whole group equivalent to the symmetric group on the set of defining coordinates. This latter aspect is also achievable through an alternative, more intricate path involving the fundamental theorem of the group. Reconstructing cosmological parameters relying on the cosmological evolution of Type Ia Supernovae (SNe Ia) rely on mapping SN Ia distances being accurately calculated. As SN Ia markers explode in various environments, their luminosities may be affected by gravitational forces bending light, specifically weak lensing, which can alter the observed distance of SNe Ia. We calculated the weak lensing effect on SNe Ia distances using a comprehensive database of galaxy distributions and compared the cosmologically-induced expansion of SNe Ia with the effect of lensing distorting their luminosity. We discovered that the influence of lensing on the apparent brightness of SNe Ia is comparable to their inherent scatter, specifically 0.23 magnitudes, which is a crucial factor in determining their distances. Consequently, ignoring this effect could lead to an incorrect estimation of cosmological parameters, particularly if the SN Ia sample we are analyzing is significantly affected by strong lensing events, as this could result in an error of up to 0.5 magnitudes in the calculation of distances, and thus a 0.5% error in the hubble constant or a 1% error in the density of matter in the universe. We applied this correction to the Pantheon SN Ia sample, which led to a 0.5% decrease in the calculated density of matter in the universe. We also discovered that this correction is most pronounced for SN Ia with higher luminosities, specifically those with a luminosity greater than -19 magnitudes. We suggested methods for future observations to minimize the influence of lensing on SN Ia luminosity, specifically targeting regions of the universe with minimal galaxy distributions. The recent rise in kidney transplants coming from incompatible donors has highlighted the need for advanced allocation strategies. Incompatible transplants are often defined as those with mismatched blood types, although other factors such as differing immunological profiles may also contribute to incompatibility. In many transplant programs, waiting lists for kidneys from compatible donors are significantly longer than those for incompatible ones, raising ethical concerns about the practice of holding out for a superior match when longer-listed patients are in need. To address this issue, the concept of 'ideal acceptance' has been introduced, which can be achieved when the number of incompatible kidneys accepted does not differ significantly from the number of compatible ones. In this study, we aim to explore ideal acceptance levels in a general setting and specifically within the current kidney allocation system used in the United States. By examining these levels in relation to waiting times and patient mortality rates, we hope to gain a better understanding of the current system's effectiveness and identify areas for improvement. This could be accomplished by adjusting the system to prioritize the acceptance of incompatible kidneys, perhaps by drawing a harder line between compatible and incompatible transplants based on the level of immunological mismatch. In this study, we outline a method for determining ideal acceptance levels and illustrate its applications by analyzing recent data on kidney transplants in the United States. The results show that the current system is far from achieving ideal acceptance levels, with a significant discrepancy between the number of kidneys accepted from compatible and incompatible donors. In fact, in many situations, the difference is so substantial that it justifies concerns about equity and fairness. In these cases, prioritizing the acceptance of incompatible kidneys could potentially save the lives of many patients who are currently being denied transplants due to the lack of suitable matches. In this study, we also examine various allocation strategies that could help the system approach ideal acceptance levels, with a specific focus on the practice of designating some kidneys as incompatible due to differing immunological profiles. We believe that a more nuanced approach to this issue could be key to improving the overall efficiency and equity of the kidney allocation system. In this context, we introduce a new term, 'immunological incompatibility', which refers to the level of mismatch required to classify a transplant as incompatible. By examining the relationship between this level of mismatch and the resulting waiting times and patient mortality rates, we hope to gain a better understanding of the optimal level of immunological incompatibility and, in turn, the number of incompatible kidneys that should be accepted in order to achieve ideal acceptance levels. This study introduces a combined level-set/embedded boundary method to address surface discontinuities and boundary integration problems in fluid dynamics, particularly in the context of melting and solidification problems. A significant advantage of this combined approach is that it eliminates the need for corrective methods, thereby providing an exact and seamless integration of level-set methods with embedded boundary techniques. Using this approach, we successfully modeled the processes of melting and solidification in both two-dimensional and three-dimensional scenarios. To validate and demonstrate this method, we employed two well-established models: the Sharpe-Scheglov solidification model and the Enthalpy-Pseudoscalar method. Our results show that the combined method yields accurate and numerically stable outcomes in various melting and solidification scenarios. To further illustrate the capabilities of this method in handling complex problems, we also modeled a Stefan problem with multiple interfaces and a melting droplet in a flowing fluid. Our results agree with those obtained using other level-set methods and provide a significant improvement over them in terms of numerical stability and accuracy. To take it a step further, we also applied this method to a moving boundary problem with a convective term, for which we found an analytical solution that matches the outcomes obtained using other level-set methods. To facilitate implementation, we also introduced a novel third-order upwind interpolation scheme, which can be used in level-set methods and other similar techniques. To assess the numerical stability of the combined method, we also modeled a melting droplet in a flowing fluid using two different grid sizes and found that the method yields highly accurate and numerically stable outcomes even in the presence of turbulence. In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to previous messages, leading to an extremely large number of outcome paths. 
To manage this challenge, we propose a novel method where each response is 
assigned to a distinct topic, represented by a category. We define a set of 
these categories as our dialogue's framework, simplifying the outcome space 
while preserving essential dialogue characteristics. To validate our approach, we 
establish a highly branching dialogue dataset consisting of 600 diverse scenes 
and 200,000 expressed conversational paths. In contrast to static datasets 
containing multiple categories, our dataset presents a dynamic setting where 
categories continuously emerge and categories that were relevant become 
obsolate. We analyze different dialogue styles using our dataset and show that 
our method effectively recovers the underlying framework that underpins the 
conversational space. To further evaluate our method, we conduct two experiments 
where we either artificially create a static dataset from our data or generate 
a new dataset based on our dataset's structure. In both cases, our method 
successfully recovers the underlying categories and conversational structure. 
Our code and data are available at: https://github.com/TextWorld/MTD.

This research investigates an intricate problem involving acoustic forcing of a turbulent jet flame in an enclosed space. When a flame burns in an enclosed environment, it can cause the air to move and result in sound being produced. Conversely, the presence of sound can influence the flame's behavior and pose safety risks due to increased pressure. To better understand this process, an experimental setup was used to burn ethylene in an open loop system while acoustic waves were intentionally applied to the air stream feeding the flame. High-speed imaging, particle imaging velocimetry, mass flux measurement, and temperature and pressure sensors were employed to gather data on the burning process, air flow, and the resulting sound. To analyze the data, an active flame method was integrated into the $\lambda$2D framework, a comprehensive simulation tool, to model the burning process, air flow, and sound production in an iterative process. This approach allowed for the accurate reproduction of the experimental conditions. To further study the burning process, different ethylene flow rates, acoustic forcing frequencies, and forcing levels were tested in the simulation. These simulations revealed how the flow rate affects the flame's length, the distribution of heat released per unit length, and the sound frequency produced. Additionally, the results showed that acoustic forcing can result in different flame behaviors, including extension, contraction, or remaining unchanged. The data from the simulations were then compared to the data from the experimental setup, revealing that the simulations accurately replicated the experimental results. To apply this knowledge in practice, an active control approach was tested in the simulation, which showed that it is possible to reduce noise produced by the burning process. Moreover, the results highlighted the importance of considering turbulence and air flow instability when analyzing the burning process, air flow, and sound production. The research also highlighted the capabilities of the active flame method and the $\lambda$2D framework in replicating the burning process, air flow, and sound production in an enclosed environment. The findings from this research are relevant to industries that burn fuels in enclosed spaces, such as power plants and industrial facilities, where reducing noise and improving safety is crucial. The research also opens up new areas of investigation, including the study of hydrodynamics and flame dynamics in an enclosed environment and the development of noise reduction strategies in such environments. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Galactic Centre reveal sources that have remained inactive for an extended period, and are thus classified as quiescent X-ray binaries. To determine the nature of these sources, researchers studied the time spans between repetitions of 15 of these sources, using data from a 20-year archive of Chandra observations. Findings show that the recurrence periods of these sources are remarkably long, with the majority taking more than a decade to reappear, even in the presence of an all-sky X-ray survey that allows for the discovery of active sources with much shorter periods between outbursts. By comparing the distribution of these long recurrence periods to theoretical models, researchers propose that the vast majority of these sources with long recurrence periods are actually low-mass binary star systems, involving a neutron star rather than a black hole. This conclusion is supported by calculations showing that such a system would require at least 10 to 20 years of inactivity, and that even then, there would be some chance of it reappearing within a decade. Furthermore, instances where the recurrence period is much shorter than a decade are thought to be influenced by recent outburst activity, leaving behind a trail of sources with longer recurrence periods in the 20-year time frame studied. Ultimately, the prevalence of these low-mass binary star systems in the Galactic Centre is notable, with estimates suggesting there are over 10 million of them in the Milky Way galaxy, based on observations and theoretical modeling, and by considering the characteristics of the active sources with shorter recurrence periods, which are similar to typical TDE and SGRB distributions, with absolute magnitudes ranging from -9 to -16, and characteristic outburst durations of a few months to a year.

When examining conversations between humans, it becomes apparent that interlocutors frequently hold distinct understandings and definitions for the same term or concept.  This variety in semantics often finds a way to coexist and even proves beneficial in discussions, reflecting the intricate relationship between language, knowledge, and reality.  Our research seeks to explore and quantify the prevalence of such semantic diversity within conversations.  To achieve this, we employ a tool with a wide range of annotated statements and definitions, drawing from a comprehensive dataset of natural language inference, and then design an evaluation framework that assesses the variety of definitions for a given term or concept based on its ability to distinguish related statements, utilizing a critical threshold to gauge the minimum degree of diversity required.  We also introduce a novel metric, the semantic diversity coefficient, which provides a compact and interpretable measure of this variety.  Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate how the coefficient varies across different conversation topics and showcase its capability in identifying definitions that exhibit a high level of diversity, as evidenced by statements that were previously unknown to our NLI dataset.  Our findings have significant implications for the development of more sophisticated conversational agents, given the inevitable presence of semantic variety in definitions and conversations.  We hope this research will serve as a foundation for a broader investigation of the complex and dynamic nature of language and knowledge.  For the sake of clarity and convenience, we have made our code available to the public domain.  We have also presented our results at the ACL 2021 conference during the seminar titled "The Silent assumption of monosemous words in word-definition tasks" in the semiotic section.  In the report, we delved into the underlying reasons for the difficulty that deep learning models encounter when attempting to grasp the concept of semantic variety, as well as the possible strategies that these models can employ to overcome this challenge, by drawing analogies with two individual subtasks that make up the broader task of natural language inference, and conversational interactions that involve word definitions. By applying knitting links in different orientations, we observe the emergence of complex electronic patterns, both locally and system-wide. A particular arrangement of knitted links is shown to create an enormous gap at the Fermi level, potentially allowing for a wide range of electronic properties, including half-metallicity, ferromagnetism, and robust quantum phase transitions. Our theoretical findings are further validated by available experimental data, and we propose feasible methods to demonstrate the predicted effects experimentally. Moreover, we outline potential applications arising from the unique properties of strongly linked knitted metals. Our work also emphasizes the significance of accurate lattice vector identification in identifying the key features of knitted metals. Lastly, we discuss the interplay between knitted link interactions and possible phason instability, as well as the associated phonon and electron dynamics. Our calculated knitted link parameters can serve as guidelines for future experimental synthesis, and we enumerate various knitted arrangements waiting to be explored. Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $n$-gram base without altering the neural model. Through extensive experiments on tasks including language modeling, machine translation, and summarization, our hybrid approach consistently delivers enhanced performance over standard neural models and facilitates seamless domain adaptation by simply swapping the $n$-gram base, eliminating the need for additional training. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on predicting two overlapping faces from a single image, with one face oriented towards the front and the other towards the back. By casting face orientation as a binary classification problem, we establish a standard baseline using two separate classifiers, one for each orientation. However, this simple model struggles with low-resolution images and excessive pose flexibility. To enhance classification accuracy and address these limitations, we introduce a self-alignment mechanism and a quality estimation module to eliminate unnecessary posterior probabilities corresponding to incorrect orientations. Furthermore, to account for images featuring large head orientations, we introduce a model capable of predicting two facing quads, with the option to fix one quad in a standard orientation. Our approach has been applied to the LFAD dataset with promising results, achieving a 10% reduction in error rate compared to the current state-of-the-art. Moreover, our method has been evaluated on the AFLW2000-3D dataset and the ATRC dataset, also yielding superior performance in terms of precision and reconstruction quality indicators. Our code has been made publicly available at: https://github.com/ctang116/face-reconstruction-SADRNet.

Compression of perturbations requires a second period of inflation to follow the initial one, which must occur in a regime where the scalar density is significantly weakened. In both cases, we determine the relevant PBH mass ranges and find that they align with forecasts for gravitational wave observatories, such as LISA, with the added distinction that the predicted masses depend on specific observatory sensitivities. In this research, we examine a linear model that is temporally structured, meaning it follows a sequence of observations where the sample size varies, and we investigate how model parameters are estimated based on historical data to predict future observations. This analysis applies to models where the number of features exceeds the number of observations, a common scenario in high-dimensional data analysis. We show that due to the temporal nature of the data and certain regularization techniques, such models can exhibit benign overfitting when estimating the mean of future observations. Conversely, we also establish conditions under which models do not exhibit benign overfitting, in addition to a phenomenon called interference overfitting that can occur. Moreover, we explore a specific regularized linear model and establish the minimax optimal rate of estimation for the mean of future observations, demonstrating that the proposed method is optimal in a variety of scenarios. Furthermore, we provide numerical examples to illustrate the performance of this model, including both large-scale simulated data and real-world time series data. This research was presented at the Conference on Machine Learning and Applications in 2022. The proposed method has been updated to include additional results, with a special focus on the linear model without dependence on the index, where we demonstrate that due to the non-degeneracy of the design matrix, the rate of estimation can be as low as $O(\sqrt{d_n^2/n_t}$, a rate that is comparable to the best possible rates for regularized linear estimation when the number of features exceeds the number of observations. This finding can be achieved by re-defining the notion of benign overfitting as the situation where the rate of estimation is driven primarily by the eigenvalue spectrum of the design matrix rather than the noise level, a condition that is referred to as strong non-degeneracy in this research. The main contribution of this research is a detailed analysis of temporal linear models with over-parameterization, with the additional contribution of a regularized linear model without dependence on the index, with both results offering a unique insight into the phenomenon of benign overfitting. This research provides numerical examples to illustrate the performance of the proposed method in both simulated and real-world time series data, with the code available online. This research also discusses two important extensions to the proposed method, with the first extension applying to the linear model without dependence on the index, with the second extension related to the estimation of the optimal regularization parameter, with both extensions offering a valuable insight into the performance of the proposed method. A key challenge in the integration of renewable energy sources lies in managing seasonal fluctuations, which can be addressed through advanced storage systems. As storage technology improves and the cost decreases, there's a growing interest in community storage initiatives. In decentralized markets, individual households own the storage units, and a centralized authority manages them. This leads to concerns about trustworthiness, as personal data and storage devices are accessible to an external entity. To tackle this trust issue, a new self-planning storage management approach is proposed, relying on localized information and automatic software tools. The proposed method, Cautious Self-Planning, optimizes storage usage based on different scenarios of renewable energy generation and consumption, without revealing sensitive information to an untrusted third party. The results show that this approach outperforms a decentralized, trust-based solution in most cases, while also reducing data transmission requirements. The proposed algorithm also scales efficiently, enabling feasible computations for large amounts of data. The findings support the integration of community storage initiatives, making them more practical and feasible in the present day. The proposed Cautious Self-Planning method can be applied to various scenarios, including individual household storage, agricultural storage, and community storage systems, among others. The approach is adaptable to different environments and can be developed further to accommodate new storage technologies and decentralized markets. The results of the research have been utilized to create a storage planning application, available online for public use. The application receives local weather forecasts and renewable energy generation data from the household, using this information to plan optimal storage usage without the need for an external authority. The application is compatible with various operating systems and storage devices, enabling secure and reliable storage planning in decentralized markets. The proposed approach has been compared to a trust-based solution in different scenarios, with the results showing that the cautious self-planning approach reduces data transmission requirements and enhances data security, in addition to minimizing storage usage and maximizing renewable energy consumption. The approach has also been found to be energy and computationally efficient, with the results available in the paper available for public use. The paper concludes by outlining possible future developments and adaptations of the cautious self-planning approach, including but not limited to the integration of multiple objectives, time-of-use pricing, seasonal storage, and pumped storage hydro power, among others. This paper delves into the underlying causes for the limited success of distant similar learning methods. It appears that current approaches are unable to effectively tackle classification problems at the scale of ImageNet, due in part to the compression of class information that occurs when using them. Our research involves reducing complex class distances to more manageable similarities, and we find that this approach outperforms traditional methods in various classification settings, including both distant similar learning and conventional techniques. Specifically, our method excels at determining highly confident positive classifications, while also demonstrating utility in identifying negative examples and categorizing unknown samples. Ultimately, we demonstrate the scalability and efficiency of this approach by applying it to the massive ImageNet dataset. In particular, we utilize a dataset that consists of a 10-member subset from the 2,500-class ImageNet, and after conducting an exhaustive search for the ideal parameter settings, we achieve an accuracy rate of 48.3% in a single trial. In contrast, traditional distant similar learning methods struggle to surpass an accuracy rate of 40% in our experiments. To address the problem of quark flavor identification in proton-nucleus collisions, we develop a statistical method that utilizes information about the initial state proton-nucleus collisions, combined with measurements from the final state. This approach is tested using simulations of proton-proton and proton-lead collisions at the Large Hadron Collider's energy levels. Furthermore, we demonstrate how the method's inputs can be modified to investigate the flavor dependence of nuclear saturation momentum through the study of top-quark production in proton-lead collisions. Specifically, we analyze the $t\bar{t}$-pair production cross-section and the top-quark $p_T$ spectrum in various quark generation scenarios. Additionally, we discuss the potential for measuring the electric charge of top quarks in proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider's high-luminosity upgrade phase, where the method could be sensitive to the QCD nonperturbative effects arising from the initial state. In such a case, we anticipate a possible cross-section modification of $\Delta \sigma/\sigma \approx 6\%$ for $t\bar{t}$ production, along with a $p_T$ distribution shift of $\Delta p_T \approx 0.3$ GeV for top quarks, given the assumed range of the nuclear saturation momentum's magnitude. In the high-luminosity upgrade context, the top-quark charge could be determined by combining the $t\bar{t}$ cross-section and $p_T$ spectrum measurements, yielding a charge value with an uncertainty of approximately $0.5\%$. In the process, we discuss the relevant theoretical and experimental considerations. Finally, we outline the strategies for implementing these methods at future colliders, such as the Future Circular $e^+e^-$ collider or the Large Hadron Electron Collider, which offer even greater opportunities for investigating the top-quark generation and initial state QCD phenomena. The developed statistical framework is generally applicable to quark flavor identification problems in proton-nucleus collisions and can be adapted for the study of other quark flavors, such as charm and strange quarks, as well as the strange baryon, via different final-state particles. The approach based on the $t\bar{t}$-pair production cross-section and the top-quark $p_T$ spectrum is particularly effective for exploring the flavor dependence of nuclear effects and initial state QCD nonperturbative effects, even in the absence of theoretical saturation momentum models. Differential secrecy in databases and graphs has long been a subject of interest to prevent unnecessary inference of a user's private information. As networks and organizations are often represented by complex graph structures, incorporating nodes, edges, and attributes, researchers have found ways to apply differential secrecy to these structures, ensuring that attributes of a user cannot be inferred from nearby nodes. This text reviews the various methods used to maintain differential secrecy on graphs, examining the different approaches that have been proposed, such as utilizing cryptographic methods, altering attributes based on accessibility, and implementing policies, and also delves into the challenges and potential applications in this domain. Further, this text is organized by examining the numerous graphs that have been studied, including subgraphs, graphs with hidden edges and nodes, large-scale graphs, and weighted graphs, with an emphasis on the respective algorithms and protocols used for each. This review also touches on the contrasting perspectives of users and organizations, highlighting the importance of cooperation between them in promoting differential secrecy. Finally, this text concludes by examining the existing research through the lens of taxonomy, analyzing the various methods used and presenting some statistical data on the types of graphs and used algorithms used in this domain. This review is expected to provide a comprehensive understanding of the complex and diverse field of differential secrecy on graph-structured information for experienced and novice researchers alike. Exact computation in graphical models is highly efficient when the models are structured as treedynamics, thanks to the fast function evaluation allowed by their topology. However, models based on biological processes, which are often represented as directed acyclic graphs, require a more complex computation, involving the sum-product or max-product algorithm, to carry out inference or optimization. Our work presents a new, faster algorithm for both inference and optimization on directed acyclic graphs, by utilizing a simplified function description. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by applying it to the analysis of genetic regulatory networks, specifically the toolbox provided by the GenoSecQuEr platform, and show that it offers a significant improvement over existing methods. Our novel algorithm can be incorporated into existing frameworks, and we believe it has utility beyond biological applications. All necessary code has been made publicly available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/Amir-Team/DFR-Code. All necessary metadata for the model used in our experiments, along with the results and the GenoSecQuEr platform, is available at the following link: https://amrresearchgroup.org/software/dfr/. We hope this work and the associated tools will contribute to the advancement of both biological and non-biological research domains. Our new algorithm, called the Brief Function Description (BFD) framework, incurs a setup cost equivalent to $O(n)$, where $n$ represents the number of variables in a model, and a subsequent computation cost of $O(m)$ for each iteration, where $m$ represents the number of children for each variable. We further show that the BFD framework can be combined with both dynamic programming and linear programming, without incurring any additional costs. The efficacy of the BFD framework is demonstrated through the analysis of both synthetic models and a real-world genetic regulatory network, following the setup of an earlier reference. The resulting code for the models used in our experiments, along with the BFD framework and the GenoSecQuEr platform, is available at the following link: https://amrresearchgroup.org/software/dfr/. We believe that the BFD framework offers utility for any research that involves the use of structured models based on treedynamics, without biological constraints. The name of the tool used in our experiments, called GenoSecQuEr, is an automatic generator of logical rules and prioritized planning graphs, without any requirement for the intervention of its users, and it is available at the following link: https://amrresearchgroup.org/software/genes

When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of viscoelastic materials undergo shear thickening, a sudden and extreme increase in resistance to flow, often resulting in a vortex instability and the development of granular flows, as seen in simulations and experiments.  A team has recently developed a multi-scale model incorporating hydrodynamic theory and thermodynamics to explain the micro-scale collisions that cause shear thickening.  By applying this model to simulate shear thickening transitions, the researchers found that it could accurately predict the scaling of stress fluctuations in multiple shear thickening regimes, including primary and secondary shear thickening transitions.  Their simulations revealed the presence of unstable flow in the initial transition stage and showed that the model's stress fluctuations could be reinterpreted using a map of stable and unstable flow regimes scaled by particle diameter.  By further analyzing their data, the researchers discovered that stress fluctuations follow a universal pattern that can be applied to a wide range of shear thickening transitions, spanning different particle sizes, speeds, and stress levels.  This pattern consists of a brief, initial transitional phase followed by a secondary phase that takes on a specific form in the stress-speed regime scaling.  The model has been successfully integrated into the Levey-Pauly law, which describes the relationship between shear rate and friction angle, accurately capturing the scaling of stress fluctuations in multiple shear thickening regimes.  As a result, this multi-scale model provides a comprehensive and far-reaching explanation for the scaling of shear thickening transitions, offering valuable insights that can be applied to a wide range of materials and scenarios.  The researchers have also demonstrated the practical utility of this model by using it to simulate simulations and experiments conducted on cornstarch in water and silica particles in glycerol, respectively.  By further analyzing their data, the researchers found that the stress-speed regime scaling contains sufficient information to determine the conditions necessary for a material to exhibit a particular shear thickening transition, including primary and secondary transitions, as well as granular flow.  The material can then be manipulated to meet these conditions, allowing the researchers to switch the material from one state to another simply by changing speed.  The model has a wide range of applications, including the efficient transportation of suspensions, the proper placement of sprinkler systems, and the design of safer and more efficient industrial processes involving the use of viscoelastic materials. This study examines the extent to which accountants' knowledge and experience are impacted by Google's Web search results customization. A hypothetical scenario was used to test the hypothesis that tailored search results may lead to the missed inclusion of relevant information. The study found that the amount of overlooked information can be substantial, with an average of 24.5% of participants failing to discover a relevant result that would have been visible to a non-personalized search user. This study's findings have implications for organizations that rely on shared knowledge and provide search engines for their employees in the hope of promoting collaboration and information sharing. The study's results are relevant to a broader context, with implications for how Web search personalization affects work and collaboration in various professions. A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-corrected, four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial for various medical applications including imaging of organs and tissues within the body.  Following an introduction to the image formation process and technical specifications of the sequence, the proposed method involves retreating the raw data from the MRI measurements using a combination of spatial and temporal reconstruction techniques, specifically a low-rank algorithm and a Bayesian approach, to accurately reconstruct images despite respiratory movement interference.  Assessment of the sequence is achieved through evaluation of its technical performance, image quality comparison with a reference standard, and potential uses in medical research with particular focus on imaging of organs and tissues within the body.  Further advancements in data processing and analysis, combined with potential applications in MRI design, including validation of motion-corrected image reconstruction using artificial respiratory data, are also presented.  The proposed method has been successfully implemented and tested on a range of respiration patterns, as well as a segment of the abdomen in a particular MRI scan, with results demonstrating improved image reconstruction in noisy, low-resolution data with moderate respiratory movement. The fabric space |M| associated with a given piecewise linear manifold M has been an interesting concept with numerous applications, particularly in surface modeling and imaging. This paper acts as an introduction to using the fabric space in the context of a specific manifold, particularly those defined by a single complex that changes over time. We establish a connection between the fabric space and the collection of that manifold's complex variations. This connection is represented as a sub-space |M|/σ of the fabric space |M| for each σ in the collection of complexes that make up the manifold. We also introduce the concept of a fabric evolution, characterized by a set of complex variations and their corresponding sub-spaces in the fabric space. This definition enables the tracking of a manifold's topological changes over time. Furthermore, we provide a method for constructing a piecewise linear approximation of a surface from the fabric evolution, and discuss the theoretical foundations of this construction process. Additionally, we offer a practical algorithm for implementing this process. The proposed approach has been applied to real-world data, yielding promising results. The code associated with this paper is available online at https://github.com/PMoussa/PurePython_3D_Surface_Reconstruction. By focusing on the Higgs pair channel with the two Higgs masses being less than 1 TeV, we determine the present limitations on Higgs effective operators and predict that in 30 TeV colliders, even with present constraints, the discovery of certain Higgs interactions will be straightforward, with a double Higgs production cross-section of at least one femtobarn. The findings highlighted in this study also pertain to proton-proton colliders with stransverse energy of 30 TeV, although the primary focus is on TeV-level $e^+e^-$ colliders that are more sensitive to heavy Higgs bosons and multi-Higgs production processes. We perform a direct variation of parameters to obtain the classical Lagrangians for all gravity theories in (2+1) dimensions by modifying the Einstein tensor within the Einstein-Hilbert Lagrangian framework. Our approach, which avoids expansion of the Einstein tensor, allows for a clear interpretation of the resulting Lagrangians. We demonstrate that our method yields an extensive list of Lagrangians, including those for topologically nontrivial spaces, cosmological constants, and parity-breaking terms, among others. By utilizing this approach, we derive new Lagrangians that have not been previously reported in the scientific literature. Additionally, our method provides insights into the relationships between different Lagrangian densities, such as Weyl's conformal anomaly, and demonstrates that conformally anomalous terms can be obtained through direct variation of parameters. We further examine the implications of our results on the classical field equations and demonstrate that they lead to the classical Euler-Gauss Bonnet equations. Furthermore, we show that our results can be applied to (3+1) dimensional gravity, although they do not yield novel Lagrangians due to the simplicity of Einstein's equations in this dimension. Our approach also allows us to investigate the underlying symmetries of Einstein's gravity in the Lagrangian framework, which we find to be characterized by a specific set of Weyl transformations that act as the gauge symmetry of the gravitational field. We conclude by discussing the connections between our results and earlier research on the subject, including but not limited to the work of other scientists. Our findings are applicable to both pure gravity and Einstein's gravity with a cosmological constant. We end by examining the implications of our results on the topology of spacetime and provide a list of the derived Lagrangian densities in the appendix. We investigated the drag experienced by a cylindrical object moving through a layer of granular material, specifically focusing on the effect of orientation and whether the grains are loose or compacted. This study considered a two-dimensional model where the cylindrical body moves horizontally through a layer of granular material, both on the surface and saturated with a fluid. Using high-speed imaging, we were able to precisely measure the cylindrical body's drag force and the surrounding grain dynamics in detail. Notably, our findings showed that the cylindrical body experiences a rotating force, or torque, due to the uneven distribution of grains and fluid on its upper and lower surfaces. This is an important discovery because it challenges the long-held assumption that the orientation of an object moving through a fluid does not affect the torque it experiences. Moreover, this phenomenon varies greatly, not only with the orientation of the cylindrical body but also with its depth and the speed at which it moves. To further understand this behavior, we analyzed the grain and fluid dynamics around the cylindrical body, revealing that the torque it experiences is caused by the differences in fluid and grain dynamics on its upper and lower surfaces. This includes the formation of granular layering, sedimentation of grains, and the development of vortices and fluid flow. This comprehensive knowledge is crucial for accurately predicting the motion and orientation of cylindrical objects moving through fluid-saturated granular media. This research was published in the journal Physical Review Letters in 2020. Since then, we have continued to investigate similar movements with a spherical body, as well as its interaction with loose and saturated granular layers, and have found similar anisotropic effects on its drag and orientation. We have also discovered that a spherical body experiences oscillatory motion when moving through a saturated granular layer, caused by the sudden release of energy as grains and fluid interact and change position around it. This movement varies depending on its size, the speed at which it moves, and the depth of its movement. Notably, this anisotropic effect persists even when the spherical body moves through a loose layer of grains, although it is much less pronounced. This is an important finding because it shows that even in loose environments, objects can experience anisotropic effects, which could have significant implications for our understanding of the motion of objects through real-world environments, including sand and other granular materials, on land and in water. This discovery could also have applications in fields such as sports and game strategy, where the orientation of objects, such as balls, can affect their movement and interaction with their surroundings.
