A superdiffusive transport model is often characterized by a mean-square displacement that exceeds linearly with time, beyond the linear diffusion phase. In this study, we investigate the spatial and temporal variability of an open random medium's permeability to explore the fundamental aspects of diffusion. We determine the specific parameters of Gaussian distributions that represent the spatial variability of permeability and use them to calculate the average and fluctuation of the mean-square displacement as functions of time and the standard deviation of the log-normal distribution of permeability. Our results show that the average mean-square displacement is directly proportional to the square of the average log-scale factor of the diffusion medium, the Harvitz mean of the log-scale factor, or the second moment of the log-scale factor. However, the standard deviation of the mean-square displacement exhibits a more complex relationship with the standard deviation of the log-scale factor, behaving as if it were proportional to the square root of the average log-scale factor, or requiring a model that accounts for the log-scale distribution's skewness. We discuss the applicability of these results to various models of permeability variability and the difficulties of inferring the log-scale distribution of permeability from mean-square displacement data alone. Furthermore, we highlight the challenges of predicting diffusion's asymptotic behavior based solely on average and variability of the mean-square displacement. In addition, we analyze the standard deviation of the mean-square displacement's logarithm as a measure of its asymptotic behavior's variability and show that it can be as difficult to predict as the average log-scale factor, requiring a model that accounts for the log-scale distribution's skewness, even in the presence of a well-defined diffusion asymptote. In such cases, the standard deviation of the mean-square displacement's logarithm will eventually converge to a constant value, albeit with a long characteristic time that is difficult to predict, due to the complexity of the log-scale distribution and the resulting difficulties of predicting the standard deviation of the mean-square displacement's logarithm's variability, the average log-scale factor, and the standard deviation of the log-scale distribution, all of which combine to determine the mean-square displacement's variability, as measured by the coefficient of its logarithm. In the process, we also derive a specific log-normal distribution of permeability that results in a mean-square displacement that is directly proportional to the square of the time, as has been observed in some experiments, and provide a diffusive effective medium theory explanation for this behavior, as has been previously proposed, but now proven through an exact calculation of the mean-square displacement distribution.

A fundamental theory is developed to describe the interplay between linear and Kerr nonlinear patterns in dielectric optical resonators, allowing for both axisymmetric and patterned situations. This approach, a significant advancement over previous work, incorporates a novel dimensionless parameter that bridges the gap between linear and nonlinear regimes. By applying a multiple-scale expansion in relation to this tiny nonlinear dimensionless quantity, a perturbation expansion is performed to predict the behavior of resonating microstructures. Emphasizing both theoretical and practical significance, the analysis delves into the intricate dynamics of resonators, revealing the intricate relationships between linear and nonlinear patterns, as well as their coupling. Furthermore, this framework facilitates a deeper understanding of waveguide and resonator patterns, revealing the essential dimensions required for stable nonlinear localized modes. Moreover, the theory provides a precise prediction of the critical dimension where linear patterns become unstable and nonlinear patterns emerge. Additionally, the analysis reveals the effects of curvature on pattern stability or instability in resonators. This theoretical framework has been tested against numerical solutions, offering a versatile and universal tool for predicting the nonlinear patterns in a wide range of optical systems. Dynamic processes, continually updated and evolving over time, pose a significant challenge for correct and efficient performance. As processes are subject to flux, traditional approaches to verification and optimization become less effective. To address this, we develop an exploration strategy that adapts to changing processes, combining the methods of verification and exploration in a unified framework. Our approach ensures correctness and minimizes the changes to processes, leading to a more scalable and efficient solution. We also leverage a streamlined representation, known as a path log, to represent processes, further improving performance. Our implementation, available as the Peval platform, supports the evaluation of dynamic processes and provides user-friendly APIs for problem definitions and processes in the form of path logs. We showcase Peval's capabilities across a range of applications, from declarative languages to learning and verification tasks. By transforming processes into streams, we can also utilize existing stream processing engines, generating efficient and scalable solutions for processes that evolve over time. In our evaluation, we discovered a nearly three-fold improvement in performance when processes are dynamic. To handle processes that are highly complex and unpredictable, we introduce a new approach based on a stream-based representation, exploring a limited aspect of processes while ignoring irrelevant parts, and only updating process validation when necessary. This strategy leads to a significant further reduction in performance costs when processes are extensively varied. We also provide a detailed comparison of our stream-based approach with a more conventional solution, demonstrating both the efficiency and the limitations of our method. To handle processes that are both dynamic and massive in scale, we propose a hybrid solution, combining the stream-based approach with a more conventional solution, dividing processes into smaller, more manageable pieces to further reduce performance costs. We conclude by outlining potential future enhancements and our plan for making Peval available as an open-source platform. We have previously published preliminary aspects of Peval in the form of papers at an ICSME workshop and an ICSE workshop, respectively. In the evaluation section, we include a comparative analysis with a more conventional solution, as well as a discussion of the challenges and limitations of our approach, and provide detailed implementation details of Peval. We also include an appendix that includes an overview of the relational logic language, the definition of process validity, the specification of exploration strategies, the description of process change streams, the definition of learning tasks, the specification of declarative languages, and the description of learning algorithms. We examine the extension of Grothendieck's algebraic compactification concept to geometric purity, and explore its applications, particularly in establishing the existence of compactifications for certain moduli spaces through the use of Hodge theory. We also discuss the connection to Luna's geometric compactifications, formed via blow-ups in invariant theory. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between these compactifications, and the boundary of which contains the original moduli space. This space is known as the boundary chamber, and its study relies on geometric pure compactifications. We also touch on the related concept of the Chow group, and provide an example based on the compactification of the space identifying lines in a projective space. This example demonstrates the involvement of the Weyl group arising from the symmetry group action, as well as the role of geometric pure compactifications in removing the components added by the blow-up process that do not contribute to the boundary chamber. This is in contrast to the approach using Hodge theory, which removes components based on the index of the associated cycle map, specifically those with a non-trivial kernel. To determine the effectiveness of X-ray images in tracking the progression of COVID-19 through machine learning, we need a well-established measurement tool.  To address this need, we established and tested an automated metric that assesses the change in images over time, with applications in following the progression of COVID-19 on X-ray images and in evaluating features extracted from convolutional neural networks.  Our research utilized a large dataset of lung X-ray images associated with patient data, including age, sex, treatment in an ICU, death status, and laboratory results. This paper delves into the source of low performance in VRD tasks due to a high rate of erroneous positive annotations. To overcome this challenge, it suggests that the VRD task be viewed as a two-class problem, separating valid relationships from ineffective ones. To demonstrate the significance of this approach, it is shown that traditional methods fail to distinguish between accurate and inaccurate annotations. To tackle this issue, a novel technique is developed, prioritizing the identification of incorrect annotations as positives. The proposed method, named Relationship Rejection, leverages a dual-learning framework that combines two classification tasks: one identifies valid relationships as positive, and the other identifies incorrect annotations as positive. Relationship Rejection achieves superior performance in the VCR dataset and sets a new standard for evaluation metrics. Furthermore, it highlights the importance of correctly classifying difficult examples, and provides a tool to pinpoint challenging instances in any dataset. A recent observation of a massive hot dense spin of a solar-type star, likely the result of a planetary disruption, has sparked interest in understanding the potential for planets to exist in the star's inner zone. To combat the instability that inner planets cause by triggering corotation instability and mass loss, a conservative model suggests they must be positioned at a 20-degree slope from the equator. However, by assuming a uniform distribution of angular momentum, we find that this threshold can be much higher, potentially allowing planets to exist closer to the star. When considering the effects of migration, a gentle slope might be sufficient to prevent mass loss, allowing planets to settle in the inner zone, and facilitating the formation of exoplanets similar to those found by Kepler. Additionally, we discuss possible mechanisms for transferring angular momentum to the star's surface and sinking its rotation, and examine the potential for it to occur in other stars, offering a distinguishing feature visible in their light spectra. If confirmed, this could provide a means of indirectly detecting dense planets in the star's inner zone, offering insights into their existence and influencing their formation. Lastly, we discuss possible variations in planetary formation that could prevent the formation of dense planets in the inner zone, offering a potential explanation for the limited range of stars exhibiting this phenomenon. Ultimately, this leads to a broader understanding of the interplay between angular momentum, mass loss, and planetary formation, and highlights the importance of considering all forms of mass loss and angular momentum, including those caused by magnetic activity and mass loss, in your analyses.

A special case of NGCPs, defined as "polyphase Golay complementary sets" (PGCSs), is then introduced. PGCSs can be created using NGCPs and an arbitrary sequence. This distinction makes them part of a more exclusive group, as only a finite number of star normal quotient diagrams exist outside of the twisted wreath type. Our findings also imply that another distinct group, composed of locally arbitrary binary systems from the generalized twisted wreath type, contains an infinite number of structures. Both of these infinite groups have previously unreported properties and exist within the broader context of a specific kind of mathematical system called a partial group. Our work builds upon a previous discovery by the paper's second author, who found a single infinite family of partial groups with a specific property, referred to as the twisted wreath type. This property can be applied to a variety of mathematical disciplines, including combinatorial geometry, algebraic geometry, and statistical mechanics. The paper's results were previously presented at two academic conferences: the International Conference on Discrete Mathematics and Theoretical Computer Science, and the Workshop on Algebraic and Combinatorial Methods in Computational Geometry. Our work also establishes connections to two other families of structures: the infinitely large families of partial groups known as the $3$-twisted wreath groups and the locally arbitrary binary systems known as the random field models. These connections are achieved through various definitions and properties, including the notion of a closed subset, the structured pair property, the compatibility of branches, the compatibility of vertices with branches, and the value function. Our work demonstrates that both the star normal quotient diagrams and the partial groups can be constructed using a process called the group generation procedure, which involves a complex algorithm that starts with random starting parameters and generates a sequence of approximate solutions through the use of a variety of subroutines, including the branch extraction subroutine, the branch merging subroutine, the junction extraction subroutine, and the junction merging subroutine. Our paper provides a detailed analysis of this algorithm and its resulting structures, which are mathematical in nature and applicable to fields such as discrete mathematics, theoretical computer science, algebraic geometry, and statistical mechanics. Our work offers theoretical and practical solutions to a variety of problems, including a combinatorial problem known as the minimum edge length arrangement, a geometric problem known as the minimum gap problem, a discrete optimization problem known as the tree decomposition problem, a complex system known as the random field model, and a computational problem known as the group generation problem. Recent advances in large language models have achieved high performance on numerous natural language processing tasks, surpassing the capabilities of traditional machine learning methods. Despite this progress, many challenges remain in leveraging these models for real-world applications. Current approaches often rely on vast amounts of data to train models, without sufficient consideration for integrating structured information essential for effective operations. This work presents a novel framework, Ability, that enables the incorporation of structured knowledge into large language models through a knowledge graph, leading to improved performance in various tasks. We demonstrate the advantages of our framework by incorporating structured knowledge from Wikipedia into LLMs, resulting in substantial gains in information retrieval-related tasks, including berkeley facts, wiki links, and wiki summary generation. Specifically, our findings show that Ability outperforms baseline models by 9.5% and 12.3% in berkeley facts and wiki links, and 13.6% in wiki summary generation, respectively. Furthermore, our approach proves versatile, accommodating diverse knowledge structures and scalable, with manageable computational requirements. By launching an open dataset for evaluating the effectiveness of knowledge graphs in information retrieval-related tasks, we aim to contribute to the development of more comprehensive assessment methods for evaluating the capability of LLMs in incorporating structured information. All code and datasets used in this study are available at https://github.com/thu-glue/Ability.

This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. The efficacy of a numerical method is typically assessed based on its ability to maintain accuracy in the presence of large time steps and small time increments. However, such an assessment may not consider the impact of round-off error caused by the method's formulation. For example, the Euler method exhibits the round-off error issue when used to solve an ODE with a large time step, although it can still deliver precise results when the time step is modest. To address this limitation, we develop a decoupling technique that separates the efficacy of a numerical method into two parts: the effect of round-off error and the impact of small time increments. Specifically, this technique provides an upper bound on the round-off error caused by the method and identifies conditions under which this upper bound remains narrow. We further illustrate the decoupling approach by applying it to the Euler method. In this case, the decoupling technique confirms that the Euler method has limited round-off error and only exhibits the big time step instability issue, as opposed to the common belief that it has limited stability in the presence of large time steps. On the other hand, the decoupling analysis shows that the Euler method does have limited stability when the time step is modest, which is in line with the existing understanding. In addition, we derive an upper bound on the round-off error caused by the Euler method and demonstrate that this upper bound remains narrow when the time step remains modest. In the process of developing the decoupling approach, we introduce the concept of a numerical method's full order and show that it is directly linked to the round-off error caused by the method. We further establish that the reduction in the numerical method's order does not influence the round-off error, which instead is determined by the method's full order and time step characteristics. We support these findings with the Euler method as an example. Finally, we explore the relationship between the numerical method's full order and the time step characteristics and provide a decoupling theorem that enables us to determine the numerical method's full order based on its efficacy in the presence of small time increments and time step characteristics. We conclude by applying this decoupling theorem to the Euler method and identifying its full order, which we find is directly linked to the round-off error caused by the method and time step characteristics. We further develop a decoupling approximation of the Euler method's full order and demonstrate that this decoupling approximation is narrow when the time step remains modest. The rising popularity of autonomous systems faces challenges due to the need for extensive training, now preventable with co-learning techniques. A way to engage autonomous agents in learning alongside humans has them interpret and repeat back their understanding of observed scenes. However, there's a more efficient method involving agents that can learn from each other after observing the same scene, without the necessity for repeated human explanation. In this research, we explore and innovate beyond this level of co-learning by developing a method called Co-Zero-Shot Learning, in which agents that have observed the same scene can learn from each other without prior knowledge. We achieve this through the integration of powerful contrastive learning and a multi-agent version of the process called Masked Multi-Agent Zero-Shot Learning. Our experiments, conducted on the CLEVR-Dataset with randomly assigned roles, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, and we also develop a version for human-agent co-learning known as Co-Observation Learning. When applied to this version, our method achieves a lower error rate compared to the baseline. Moreover, with only a single observation, our method enables agents to accurately describe scenes to each other, a level of performance comparable to the level achieved through extensive autonomous learning. In addition, we introduce a new evaluation metric known as Description Accuracy, and our method excels in scenarios with limited attribute variations. Our research presents a novel co-learning technique, and our method is applicable to various real-world scenarios, a representation of which is demonstrated through an independent simulation called Multi-Agent Scene Description. With simple yet effective modifications, we also introduce a version of our method for human-agent co-learning known as Co-Observation Learning, a name that reflects its purpose of combining co-observation and zero-shot learning. This version of our method is a groundbreaking technology, a level of performance previously unachievable in the field of co-learning. Using reinforcement learning to train neural machine translation models has shown significant improvements in translating difficult languages. However, a major limitation of current approaches remains - they only consider the source language as part of the action space, neglecting the target language. This oversight leads to several issues, including target language interference and the time-consuming process of generating a target sentence. To overcome these challenges, our research suggests that the entire action space, comprising both source and target languages, should be utilized in reinforcement learning. This is achievable by redefining the action space as a sequence of characters rather than words, which significantly expands the space to be explored. To manage this expanded space, we introduce a new policy learning objective that improves the efficiency of character-level policy learning. Our proposed approach, called Character Policy Learning (CPL), leverages a combination of maximum likelihood estimation and a contrastive unregularized term to guide efficient exploration of the action space. To further enhance performance, we integrate CPL with a range of regularization techniques, including latent variable-based methods and prefix regularization. Our experiments on translation tasks show that utilizing the entire action space and a proper regularization technique can lead to substantial gains in translation quality. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented NoSQL database that has gained
significant popularity in recent years. Despite its success, MongoDB's
transactional functionality remains poorly understood, particularly with regards
to its default isolation level, which is currently set to "session" and
equivalent to read committed in traditional relational databases. In session mode,
MongoDB uses a "sticky" snapshot of data, which remains unchanged until the
end of a transaction. Although this isolation level provides a high level of
protection against inconsistent reads, it can lead to reduced concurrency and
performance degradation. In contrast, in "transaction" mode, MongoDB uses a non
sticky snapshot that can be updated during a transaction, resulting in
increased concurrency, but with a higher risk of inconsistent reads. In this paper
we validate the theoretical analysis of MongoDB's transactions by collecting
performance data and introducing a test suite that includes both microbenchmarks
and larger-scale applications with complex workload patterns. Our results show
that in session mode MongoDB's performance degrades significantly when combining
insert and rollback operations, but improves when using distributed transactions.
On the other hand, in transaction mode the performance is generally better, but
with a significant slowdown when combining update and rollback operations. Our
analysis indicates that this slowdown is caused by MongoDB's failure to apply
efficient fixup operations following the roll back of a transaction. We also
examine the practical implications of these findings for real-world applications
that use MongoDB's transactions. In particular, we find that in session mode
MongoDB's performance degrades when combining insert and rollback operations, which
is similar to the performance slowdown introduced by Google's Spanner's default
isolation level in relational databases. In contrast, in transaction mode the
performance is generally better, but with a significant slowdown when combining
update and rollback operations. Finally, we discuss the practical implications
of these findings for real-world applications that use MongoDB's transactions. In
particular, we advise against using insert operations within transactions when
combined with rollback operations, unless absolutely necessary. We also propose
simple workarounds for both session and transaction modes that can mitigate
these performance slowdowns. In addition, we discuss the importance of
understanding the interplay between concurrency control methods, storage
structures, and workload patterns when evaluating the performance of transactions
in NoSQL key-value stores no different from relational databases. Lastly, we
report on our experience with testing and validating MongoDB's transactions, a
challenging process

We introduce a novel concept of cluster functions for quantum groups, and demonstrate that the structure of Lusztig's quantum cluster algebra is characterized by these functions. This characterization reveals the distinct features of the algebra's structure, including the location of its cluster seeds, the direction of its Weyl group actions, and the identification of invariant monodromy. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the algebra's structure and properties of its invariant functions, specifically the polynomial nature of its Eulerian elements and the additive nature of its modified Eulerian elements. These properties hold without the assumption of finite generation of the algebra's cluster algebra. We prove that the cluster characters of the algebra's finite-dimensional representations are invariant under the monodromy action induced by Weyl group elements, and provide explicit formulas for these actions. Additionally, we demonstrate that the algebra's cluster characters distinguish its finite-dimensional representations, and investigate the representation-theoretic implications of the algebra's invariant functions. Finally, we establish connections between the algebra's cluster characters and classical cluster algebras, specifically in regards to their invariant elements, and demonstrate that the algebra's cluster characters contain factors analogous to Hall-Littlewood polynomials, which are invariant under the action of the Weyl group and satisfy the orthogonality property of the quantum group. We conclude by analyzing the specific case of the $A_2$ Lie algebra, for which we determine the combinatorial structure of its cluster algebra, provide an explicit classification of its invariant functions, and characterize the representation-theoretic interpretation of these functions. We also establish connections between the algebra's cluster characters and classical Hall-Littlewood polynomials, and investigate the finite generation of the algebra's cluster algebra. Lastly, we offer a mathematical explanation for the results observed in the $A_2$ case. We compare our analysis with existing literature on the subject, for which we provide a brief overview in the paper's introduction. The study of the $A_2$ case algebra enables us to demonstrate the theoretical results mentioned above through concrete example, and to analyze the algebra's cluster characters in regards to their representation-theoretic and combinatorial properties. The paper's final section is dedicated to an overview of the research presented, as well as its connections to related topics in mathematics and physics. The study of the $A_2$ case algebra enables us to demonstrate the theoretical results mentioned above through concrete example, and to analyze the algebra's cluster characters in regards to their representation-theoretic and combinatorial properties.

Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive analysis of these schemes was previously unfeasible. However,, a prominent example called Forsage, utilizing cryptocurrency smart contracts, allows for the examination of participant interactions through access to transaction data. This paper utilizes a large dataset of nearly 50,000 Forsage participants and over 160,000 related cryptocurrency transactions to explore the underlying dynamics of a pyramid scheme. By applying network analysis and machine learning techniques, researchers reveal intricate patterns of activity among participants, exposing vulnerabilities in the design of the scheme that favor certain participants over others. Furthermore, findings reveal the spatial dissemination of the scheme among various geographic locations. A notable observation is the presence of a governing elite composed of a small group of highly influential participants who control the majority of the scheme's assets. And finally, by mapping transaction relationships among participants, researchers are able to visualize the dynamic evolution of the scheme's hierarchical structure. This study provides an in-depth look at a pioneering example of a pyramid scheme built using smart contracts, offering valuable insights that can be applied to a broader category of investment scams. This research was previously presented at the IEEE Conference on Trustcom/BigDataSE/PAAS 2021. This paper is a revised and expanded version of that work, incorporating additional analysis and results. In recent years, graph-based neural networks have gained significant traction, surpassing traditional image-based models in various applications. Our research introduces a novel learning framework called Transformation-Unique Smoothing for Point Cloud Structures, which incorporates a distinctive smoothing technique utilizing transformations that operate independently of the underlying graph structure. We found this approach to be particularly effective in smaller-dataset scenarios, including in experiments with a 20-class classification model using the ModelNet10 dataset. Nonetheless, when working with larger datasets, our results indicate that this approach's unique smoothing technique loses its advantage over conventional methods. Our novel technique is also adaptable to various graph structures and can be applied to various neural network components, including multi-layer perceptrons, fully connected layers, and layer normalization modules. By harnessing the expertise of both advisory agents and autonomous learning, our model sets multiple benchmarks in various tasks, including the SHREC non-rigid 3D object alignment challenge. Our code is now available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhou-kk/TPC. Moreover, a paper titled Consider Carefully: Strategic Selection for Neural Agent-Autonomy Hybrid Frameworks, which details a more advanced version of our earlier work, has also been published. This new work involves a method for selectively choosing between neural network-based autonomous learning and rule-based agent guidance, resulting in a hybrid framework that outperforms both pure neural network-based autonomous learning and rule-based agent guidance in various tasks. When working with smaller datasets, our research found that this approach leads to better performance, including in experiments using the ModelNet10 dataset with a 20-class classification model. When working with larger datasets, our results indicate that this approach loses its advantage over conventional methods. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) rely on two closely linked components: a generator creating data that resembles a specific target distribution and a discriminator effectively distinguishing between data drawn from this target distribution and data generated by the generator. For most applications, including those related to image processing, a dense training approach for both components has been sufficient. However, in the case of text data, a more practical approach would involve training a sparse GAN, one where the generator produces samples that are significantly different from the target distribution and the discriminator fails to successfully distinguish these samples with high confidence. We have developed an algorithm called SparseGAN that generates sparse, high-quality data. It employs an alternating descent method to handle the non-differentiable objective function associated with the confidence of the discriminator. We have also introduced a novel assessment metric that evaluates the density of the generated data. SparseGAN yields outstanding performance in various evaluations and outperforms existing methods in generating dense data. It is available on GitHub at the URL https://github.com/ShuaiNiUk/SparseGAN. We have further provided code and model downloads at the URL https://shuanik.github.io/project/SparseGAN. Leveraging SparseGAN as a tool to augment sparse data, we have conducted an experimental assessment of its performance in eight different datasets. Interestingly, when used to enhance the training set, SparseGAN significantly reduces overfitting and significantly improves the performance of five out of eight different datasets without any adjustment, largely due to its inherent ability to prevent the generator from overfitting by creating data that is more different from the target distribution. However, when used to generate dense data, SparseGAN requires a careful selection of hyperparameters to ensure that the generator produces high-quality data that is sufficiently similar to the target distribution. We have discussed two different approaches to achieve this and provided detailed results for two different datasets. Finally, we have introduced a hypothesis that SparseGAN can be used to create adversarial examples for different machine learning models, largely due to its inherent ability to produce data that is different from the target distribution. We have validated this hypothesis through an experimental assessment of SparseGAN's performance in generating adversarial examples for two different datasets. Interestingly, SparseGAN generates high-quality adversarial examples that are highly similar to the original data and can significantly reduce the performance of the corresponding machine learning models to a minimal degree. We have discussed this further and provided detailed results for two different datasets. The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of determining whether this theory is true or not. To tackle this issue, researchers propose using combination of astrobiological studies and astronomical observations to verify the hypothesis of interstellar panspermia. By examining microbial life forms that have survived on comets and meteorites, as well as identifying signs of past life on asteroids, a team from the COMET PROJECT proposes that a positive detection could be made for interstellar panspermia. To achieve this, they estimate that a capability similar to that of the ALMA telescope would be required for both biological and astronomical aspects. Furthermore, a statistical analysis of data from various comet and meteorite samples suggests that the probability of interstellar panspermia could be significant, with approximately 10% of comet samples showing evidence of having life transferred to them, and around 30% of meteorites exhibiting the same trait. To move forward, the authors advocate for a focused research effort on this subject, suggesting that a dedicated mission studying samples of comet and asteroid origins could yield a breakthrough in this area. To that end, they propose a rough estimate of what such a mission would entail. Lastly, discovering evidence of interstellar panspermia would have implications for a variety of fields, ranging from the distribution of life in the universe to the effectiveness of planetary sterilization, and potentially even combating the risk of interstellar contamination. Ultimately, as expressed by the late astronomer Carl Sagan, it is an incredible adventure worth embarking on. Animal population studies and wildlife management often benefit from a combination of two essential methods: Spatial Capture-Recapture (SCR) and Resource Selection Functions (RSF). SCR provides a superpopulation size estimate and detailed information about animal distribution patterns, while RSF identifies preferred habitats and helps predict spatial occurrence probabilities. However, these methods typically operate within separate frameworks with limited integration. Our study introduces a novel approach that combines SCR and RSF data, utilizing observed capture probabilities in a Bayesian framework to inform the RSF model and accurately estimate occurrence probabilities across the study area. We examine the challenge of developing accurate node degree estimations in a large network, given limited local view data and the presence of malicious nodes providing faulty information. We investigate the optimal number of reliable nodes required for reliable degree estimation in various network configurations. Our key discovery indicates that, with a small number of unreliable nodes, a network cannot provide accurate estimates if its diameter exceeds a specific, underlying number. We also find that the minimum required reliable nodes necessary for a correct estimation exceeds a particular value when the number of unstable nodes reaches another particular value. In a network with a large diameter, we find the minimum required reliable nodes necessary for a correct estimation to be directly proportional to its diameter. We demonstrate that, in a network with a maximum node degree of a certain value, the minimum required reliable nodes necessary for a correct estimation is also directly proportional to this value. We show that, in a random small-world graph, we can optimize the underlying number for a low-diameter feature by balancing two opposing factors: the negative impact of an overspacious network and the difficult remaking of connections between distant nodes. We develop two scalable algorithms providing degree estimation: a non-interactive 'iterative' method and an interactive 'iterative' method requiring the ability to ask questions about the network. We analyze the robustness of these algorithms in networks with a specific geometry and random small-world graphs. We compare our algorithms with the existing method of robust estimation, demonstrating our methods' superiority in networks with a large diameter. We conduct extensive simulations of random small-world graphs to test our algorithms, as well as various network configurations with various diameters, showing that our algorithms are highly reliable in managing network failures. We examine the applicability of our algorithms to large networks, concluding that, with the current computational capabilities, these algorithms may face scalability issues in very large networks. We propose several potential modifications to overcome these issues, enabling the successful application of these algorithms to extremely large networks. We also investigate the possibility of estimating networks using algorithms that can handle very large networks, proposing a novel approach based on decentralized degree estimation. We conduct simulations of our proposed approach, demonstrating the feasibility of accurately estimating a network with a large diameter. We further examine the challenge of detecting malicious nodes, proposing a method based on degree estimation, as well as a more robust version of this method, demonstrating the effectiveness of these methods in detecting malicious nodes in various network configurations. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring this quantity accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the Nernst effect in thin layers of the antiferromagnetic antiperovskite manganese nickel nitride (Mn$_3$NiN) structured in a (0 0 1) orientation, utilizing precise control of their crystal orientation to explore the anomalous Nernst effect and the related Nernst Néel signal. By combining functionalized tips in scanning tunneling microscopy, we were able to achieve a comprehensive understanding of their electronic and magnetic properties on the local and magnetic levels. By integrating these results with overall magnetic characteristics, we derived a precise estimation of the anomalous Nernst effect in these layers. Our findings indicate an unusually large anomalous Nernst effect in these layers, surpassing the magnitude of the Hall effect, and also demonstrate the direct measurement of the Nernst Néel signal, an unprecedented achievement. Furthermore, we discovered that the direction of the anomalous Nernst current can be reversed by applying a magnetic field perpendicular to the layers, achieving a complete understanding of the anomalous Nernst effect by comparing it with the Hall effect and magnetic characteristics. Our results also highlight the unique properties of Mn$_3$NiN layers, indicating that they possess both positive and negative spontaneous voltage levels, along with the unique phenomenon of the Nernst effect changing sign due to the application of a magnetic field, and suggest that these layers could serve as an ideal material for high information storage and memory components, along with their potential in thermophonic devices. Our study concluded with an examination of the theoretical explanations for these unusual phenomena, along with suggestions for optimizing the layers to enhance these anomalous effects further. Our experimental discovery of the anomalous Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN layers, coupled with its unique magnetic properties, presents a significant breakthrough that has the potential to advance the study and applications of this particular class of materials. Moreover, our findings provide a clear pathway for other researchers to investigate this phenomenon in other antiferromagnetic antiperovskite materials, along with suggestions for optimizing the layers to enhance these anomalous effects further

Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The potential breakdown of these materials under critical stress levels makes it essential to detect damage exactly.
Researchers have proposed using Genetic Algorithms in conjunction with Electrical Impedance Tomography to accurately determine the distribution of damage within composites.
In this study, different genetic algorithms were integrated with EIT, and the results showed that the combination of these methods can accurately locate and quantify damage within composite materials.
This study also highlighted issues with current solutions, such as the finite element method, particularly regarding computation and data integration.
It's been found that the combination of genetic algorithms and EIT can account for the uncertainty of scan data and image reconstructions, leading to a more precise determination of damage distribution.
This novel approach has been applied to various scenarios, including sudden impacts and long-term degradation, and has demonstrated a high level of accuracy in detecting and quantifying damage.
This study provides a starting point for further development and more complex projects, such as scaling up to three-dimensional projects. 
This research was presented at the 7th International Conference of Computational Methods and Artificial Intelligence (CMUAI 2022).

Recent advancements in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in patients with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given limited attention to restoring lower body mobility. A major limitation of existing BCIs for lower body recovery is the lack of accurate prediction of step frequencies and ambulatory states. Existing models rely heavily on invasive neural recordings from the motor cortex obtained through electrocorticogram (ECoG) techniques and often require large sets of training data. A novel model utilizing a relatively small dataset derived from the posterior parietal cortex (PPC) via ECoG recordings has been developed to achieve real-time estimation of step frequencies and ambulatory states during treadmill walking. The developed model has a high potential for application in various PPC-related disorders and spinal cord injuries, with the potential for advancement to MMC-based BCI systems following further refinement. We investigate left-invariant divisions in right-angled Artin groups (RAAGs). Our findings show that left-invariant divisions are equivalent to left-invariant subgroups that act freely on a specific graph associated with the group. This graph-dependent action is transitive, and its stabilizer corresponds to the subgroup in question. Additionally, we establish that any subgroup that generates the parent group through its group generated by its elements does not constitute a division. Furthermore, we provide examples demonstrating that the capability to define divisions is highly dependent on the underlying graph, and that it can be characterized by specific properties of that graph. In particular, we prove that a RAAG defined by a tree will have divisions if and only if its tree is bicolorable. Moreover, we establish that left-invariant means on a RAAG are equivalent to left-invariant quasimetrics that are compatible with the graph defined by its generating subgroup. This leads to the conclusion that means cannot be defined on a RAAG with a non-bicolorable tree structure. Lastly, we discuss the relationship between left-invariant divisions and the action of a RAAG on a complex consisting of circles, and we establish that this action is discrete if and only if the underlying graph is locally connected. Moreover, we prove that the structure of its circles can be determined from the underlying group structure, and that this circle complex is homeomorphic to the 2-skeleton of a bicolorable tree. This in turn implies that a RAAG is generated by a finite set if and only if its defining graph is a forest. This result can also be obtained by analyzing the action of its elements on the circle complex directly. This method was applied to both artificial and real-world data, including brain signal data during a memory game. Animals play a significant role in various ecological processes, requiring their geographical tracks to be analyzed and studied. Historically, this research relied on the first-hand accounts of hunters, scientists, and local residents, whose observations were converted into rough outline forms to illustrate migration patterns. Today, with an overwhelming amount of wildlife captured through security cameras and observational networks, there's a vast amount of footage available that can be leveraged to study animal movements automatically. This report outlines a method for automatically identifying the movement of animals from wildlife feeder cameras and presents a sample application involving the detection of elk movement in Scotland. This work is part of a larger project aimed at using cameras and citizen science to study the behavior and conservation of a declining elk population in the UK. This approach can be tailored to suit various other biological movement studies. The proposed method involves a two-step process: first, it removes non-movement biological footage, and then it maps the remaining images to represent the areas where the animals are present. The corresponding code along with sample elk movement maps are available online. This work demonstrates that biological movement can be automatically extracted from video footage, enabling further analysis of animal tracks via methods used in computational geometry. The integration of this approach with algorithms used to model animal trajectories is also discussed. The code for this project is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ahmadowildlife/detecting-biological-movement. The underlying mathematics relies heavily on computational geometry and more information on the used techniques including Delaunay triangulation, point location, and circle and line intersection detection can be found in the supplementary materials. The proposed method has significant implications for various applications including conservation biology, ecology, and agriculture, and it can be adapted to suit other contexts such as the analysis of crowd movement from security cameras. The current version of the code is optimized to handle low-resolution video footage and further optimizations are required to handle higher resolution footage. The proposed approach generates biologically meaningful data that requires validation through comparative analysis with existing methods including radio telemetry and camera traps. The integration of this approach with existing methods used to model animal trajectories and with machine learning algorithms used for data validation is also discussed in the supplementary materials. The proposed method has the potential to be scalable to handle large datasets including the recently launched IPBES report suggesting that 70\% of animal species remain untracked, and the integration of this approach with cloud computing platforms such as Amazon Web Services is also possible. Networks with random defects can convey information reliably, maintaining integrity in the presence of disorder, unlike rigid structures that can shatter under stress. Researchers have successfully employed this concept, known as ubiquity, into the design of topological metamaterials, termed Topological Anderson Conductors, which maintain zero electrical resistance when placed on a substrate with random randomness. Although microscale studies have demonstrated the occurrence of ubiquity in various materials, no one has previously studied the ubiquity that occurs on a macroscopic scale in microelectronic networks constructed from random combinations of different disorder types. Our group has created a novel type of topological material, composed of 2D silicon microelectronic arrays featuring random distribution of interface roughness and point defects across a wide range of scales, and has successfully witnessed the ubiquity that occurs on a macroscopic scale in two-dimensional silicon microelectronic networks constructed from random combinations of different disorder types. Through theoretical analysis, a classification system for networks with various types and scales of randomness has been developed, and proven to maintain zero electrical resistance across a wide range of scales. Additionally, we have found that networks with specific distribution of random defects can possess both insulating and superconducting properties simultaneously, a state known as a topological Anderson phase, and has demonstrated the occurrence of this phase in actual devices. Our discovery opens up a wide range of applications for artificial materials with robust and adaptable topological properties across various fields, from quantum computing and semiconductor manufacturing to cryptography and biomedical technologies. The concept of trims has been successfully integrated into the study of graph isomorphisms, enabling a more elementarily based characterization of isomorphism properties. Specifically, two first-order properties in the realm of graphs are considered equivalent if they possess isomorphic images; conversely, having isomorphic images implies the presence of a specific binary relation called trims, which can be defined using a particular logical formula. A further advancement is achieved in this study, where it is demonstrated that the existence of isomorphic images from a given property can be determined through an examination of that property's trims in relation to its elementary class, and this classification can be achieved via a specific two-class structure defined by a particular property called finiteness. Additionally, both a special case study of connected graphs and a more comprehensive analysis of general graphs are conducted to demonstrate the utility and implications of this characterization. Specifically, it is shown that for connected graphs, the property of being isomorphic to another graph is equivalent to the presence of a particular finite trims called trees, whereas for graphs in general, this property is equivalent to the presence of a complex structure known as a forest, which is defined as a collection of distinct trees, resulting in a two-class classification based on the presence or absence of trees. Furthermore, both cases demonstrate that the property of being infinite is a necessary condition for being isomorphic to another graph. A connection to a well-known theorem by Baur and Nešetřil is also established in this study. A central theorem about first-order isomorphism properties has been extensively utilized, albeit often without acknowledgment, and it is now presented in its full form, together with a recognition of its original source. A new proof of this theorem has also been found, together with some additional information about its implications, and it is now widely available for use by the scientific community. A question that remains unanswered in this study concerns the exclusion of a specific element called constants from the class of first-order isomorphism properties, and it is hypothesized that properties without constants are inherently different from properties that include constants, although this hypothesis has yet to be proven or disproven. A possible approach to achieving this proof or disproving this hypothesis has also been presented in this study. This presentation will delve into a comprehensive Monte Carlo study involving intricate quantum chromodynamics, quantum electrodynamics, and supersymmetry, focusing on a Monte Carlo event generator for particle physics known as "FeynHiggs". Initially developed to predict particle mass and scattering likelihood in the Monte Carlo Supersymmetry Working Group's "SPhT tools" ensemble, FeynHiggs has been refined to excel at on-shell Higgs mass predictions in the Monte Carlo Supersymmetry Working Group's "SPhT tools" ensemble through the application of advanced perturbative expansion techniques. By comparing predicted masses to experimental data, constraints on intricate Monte Carlo Supersymmetry Working Group's "SPhT tools" parameters can be derived from Higgs mass measurements alone. A novel feature of FeynHiggs is the capacity to rapidly compute these parameters in the Monte Carlo Supersymmetry Working Group's "SPhT tools" ensemble via a simple multiple linear regression model. Furthermore, FeynHiggs enables the generation of Monte Carlo event samples with on-shell Higgs bosons in the Monte Carlo Supersymmetry Working Group's "SPhT tools" ensemble, facilitating the development of dedicated reconstruction techniques for predicting particle masses from detector data. The significance of considering intricate Monte Carlo Supersymmetry Working Group's "SPhT tools" parameters in particle physics experiments is also discussed. In a contextual linear gambit model, agents make decisions based on a unknown parameter vector and a data set of historical contexts and rewards. This paper explores how agents can learn their parameter vectors in a decentralized way, without sharing the context, in two distinct settings. In the first setting, titled the "Gambit Learning Through Subcontexting" scenario, all agents have access to the same data set of historical contexts and rewards, and the objective is to develop a decentralized algorithm that enables agents to learn their parameter vectors simultaneously. In the first setting, a decentralized algorithm is established that converges at a rate of $O(\log T)\sqrt{T}$ in expectation for the cumulative regret over $T$ time steps. In the second setting, titled the "Decentralized Learning in a Dynamic Context" scenario, a new data set arrives at each time step, and the objective is to learn the parameter vector associated with each data set. In the second setting, an algorithm is established that converges at a rate of $O(\log T)\sqrt{T}$ in expectation for the cumulative regret over $T$ time steps. In both settings, the agents' actions are assumed to be observed by an external observer, who provides a narrow subcontext of the historical contexts, encoded in a response matrix. Our research involves examining four event shapes that are commonly used in inclusive spectra measurements, particularly in heavy-ion collisions at the Large Hadron Collider, as well as in QCD theoretical studies. We studied these shapes in relation to the average number of participants in Pb-Pb collisions at a collision energy of 2.76 TeV, using ALICE data and theoretical information on elliptic flow's dependence on cone size. Our findings were compared to theoretical predictions made using perturbative QCD and hydrodynamic models. To better understand elliptic flow's origins, we analyzed its connection to particle emission patterns, specifically in relation to the orientation of the elliptic flow and initial state conditions, as well as in relation to the overall multiplicity and cone size. Our results showed that event shapes' sensitivities to the initial state are largely independent of cone size, primarily influenced by the medium's properties, and that they are well-described by hydrodynamic models that take into account elliptic flow's fluctuations and asymmetrical emission patterns. Our study also found that the average number of participants is sufficient to describe elliptic flow's dependence on cone size, as indicated by the near-absence of influence from finite-size corrections in large-ion collisions. Nonetheless, in smaller systems like proton-proton or semi-peripheral heavy-ion collisions, finite-size corrections might play a more significant role, potentially affecting shape corrections and possible misinterpretations of data in those contexts. Our analysis highlights the importance of accurately calibrating event shapes, as well as the necessity of accounting for finite-size corrections and initial state conditions, particularly in inclusive measurements of heavy-ion collisions. As such, we suggest modifying the event shapes' engineering algorithm to make them more suitable for smaller systems and more sensitive to the medium's properties, including a new factor that directly relates shapes to the average number of participants, as well as modifications to better capture elliptic flow's dependence on cone size and initial state conditions, as described in our paper. This work investigates the extremal values of a general performance measure, which we call gamma, in a specific type of interference network. This type of network, known as the Generalized Interference Division Multiple Access (GIDMA) network, is characterized by non-negative coefficients for each pair of communicating users, with at least one coefficient being positive. We are looking to maximize gamma under the constraint of constant total transmit power. A key finding of this study is that the extremal values of gamma eventually surpass any given large number, as long as the number of users is sufficiently large. Another significant result is that the most efficient and optimal power control schemes, even if they are very complex, eventually fail to meet a certain standard for all large networks. Originally introduced by Alfred van der Poorten in 1980, the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ was a key component in his work on equations in powers of a single prime. Van der Poorten observed that if the solution set for this equation contained an infinite number of solutions with distinct values, it would imply the existence of infinitely many solutions to another equation, thereby contradicting a conjecture known as the Pascal Prime Conjecture. Building upon previous work by himself and others, the current author develops a new framework for examining the solutions to this equation. A key component of this framework is a generalization of the Bugeaud-Krikorian formula, adapted to the prime number 7. This generalized formula enables the solutions to be expressed in a specific format, with the exponent $n$ defined as the sum of three terms, each associated with a particular digit within the base $a$, $b$, and $7$. By applying this framework, the current author is able to demonstrate a significant result: there are no solutions for $a$, $b$, and $n$ that satisfy the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ with $n$ greater than 13, and where $a$ and $b$ are both less than 7, and where the base $a$ contains at least three distinct digits. This finding extends a previous result presented by the same author in his PhD thesis, where it was shown that for $n$ greater than 13, the largest possible solution for $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ is given by the value of $7^{14}$ minus the square of $484$. Quarks instead of electrons might fill a star's core, and its sound speed is a crucial factor that determines whether such a star could exist within a specific mass range. The $M_{\rm Ch}$-c4 diagram is a tool for identifying this range, as it accounts for the effects of quark matter's possible existence on a neutron star's structure. The sound speed squared (c2) is a key ingredient in this diagram's formation, and its value depends on the equation of state that describes the matter within the star. However, determining c2 requires knowledge of the sound speed's coefficients, which can be difficult to obtain from many relativistic density functional models. This paper focuses on a specific class of models called relativistic mean-field theories that facilitate an analytical calculation of c2. We develop three distinct sound speed formulas for general, strangeness-free matter and demonstrate how they can be applied to the study of neutron stars. Additionally, we examine the possible existence of strange quark stars and discuss the sound speed formulas in this context. This paper's findings also support the existence of neutron stars with masses above 2.63 solar masses, as predicted by several earlier studies. We further explore the sound speed's relationship with the bag energy density parameter and the mass gap between neutron and quark stars. This relationship reveals that the mass gap could be as narrow as 0.1 solar masses, although this estimate relies on a specific assumption about the sound speed's coefficient. We conclude by examining the paper's results in the broader context of quark matter's possible existence and stress the importance of future density functional models that accurately describe the sound speed in dense matter. This is particularly crucial for models based on Bayesian neural networks and other machine learning techniques that can be difficult to interpret. This paper's results will contribute to the development of such models and provide a deeper understanding of the sound speed's coefficients and its relationship with the mass gap between neutron and quark stars. This knowledge is essential for creating the $M_{\rm Ch}$-c4 diagram and will facilitate the study of quark matter's possible existence in the near future. To effectively address open-domain commonsense question answering, it's essential to explore how questions and statements are connected semantically. We draw from the knowledge base to frame questions and statements as pairs with a desired alignment, then leverage reinforcement learning to compare their semantic similarity and guide pre-trained models to provide high-quality question answering statements. We demonstrate this approach's value in multiple experiments, starting with evaluating semantic pairs generated automatically, followed by a comparison of our method to benchmarks in both closed- and open-domain question answering scenarios. Our results show that a simple comparison of semantic similarities suffices to achieve high performance in closed-domain settings, whereas in open-domain settings, our method exceeds the benchmarks by a significant margin when evaluating statement quality and achieves comparable results when evaluating statement diversity. When evaluating question answering accuracy alone, our method declines slightly, yet we attribute this decline to the excessive generation of repetitive statements. A major challenge in cross-training with private data for shared models arises due to differing data sets among institutions, making direct application of existing methods difficult without significant proxy data generation. Additionally, existing methods primarily focus on weighting samples rather than incorporating diverse data effectively. In response to these limitations, this paper introduces a new model training technique called "Random Stroll," which involves taking stochastic steps between institutions during training. Unlike existing methods that concentrate on local weight adjustment, Random Stroll explores diverse datasets in search of better performance, informed by an unique failure criterion that ensures step value remains beneficial. By optimizing this criterion, we derive an expression that can be efficiently computed, enabling the effortless integration of diverse datasets in a purely federated setting. Experiments conducted using real-world data sets demonstrate the superiority of Random Stroll when compared to other methods, including FedProx and FedAvg. Moreover, Random Stroll's performance in sensitive data protection scenarios remains exceptional, proving robust when compared to other methods in scenarios involving limited institutional cooperation. In summary, Random Stroll is a versatile and highly effective model training technique tailored for institutions with access to private data, without the need for significant data exchange. In addition to its public availability, the code for Random Stroll is also publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghru/RandomStroll. In conclusion, this paper demonstrates the effectiveness of Random Stroll in various scenarios, including but not limited to healthcare, where data remains highly protected and decentralized. Mental wellness within the criminal justice system has long been a pressing concern, as research highlights the substantial mental health disorders among offenders. To address this issue and potential recidivism, some countries and states are integrating mental health treatments into their criminal justice policies, often mandating therapy for convicted individuals as a condition of their sentence. This study examines the impact of required mental health treatment on the wellness and criminal behavior of individuals within the justice system, using a natural experiment in which mental health treatment was assigned to some offenders by their probation officers, often for reasons related to their case details. By leveraging a unique dataset that tracks the outcomes of over 7,500 offenders in a particular jurisdiction over a 12-year period, we are able to assess the effect of assigned treatment on their self-reported mental wellness and criminal convictions. This research provides the first empirical evidence on the effect of mandated mental health treatment, suggesting that it leads to improved mental wellness and reduced criminal convictions among offenders, with the largest benefits seen among those with more severe mental health disorders. Furthermore, we find that the primary source of these benefits lies in the reduced incidence of new convictions among individuals who complete their sentence without further convictions, highlighting the long-term impact of treatment on their behavior. We also examine the potential mechanisms through which treatment achieves these outcomes, pointing to a range of possible mental health-related effects, as well as various justice system responses that influence an individual's continued participation in the justice system. Finally, we discuss the policy implications of these findings for other justice systems, highlighting the potential for a more cost-effective approach to reducing recidivism and improving mental wellness among offenders. This could be achieved by targeting those with more severe mental health disorders, increasing the duration of treatment for those who benefit from it, and exploring ways to improve retention rates among those who drop out of the program. This research provides a valuable opportunity to learn from the experiences of other justice systems that have successfully integrated mental health treatments into their policies, offering a framework for analyzing the underlying mechanisms and outcomes of such programs, and providing a way to evaluate the impact of these programs on the wellness and criminal behavior of individuals within the justice system. Quantum systems' behavior can be highly unpredictable due to their sensitive response to initial conditions, as demonstrated in the seminal work of von Neumann and Wigner. To gauge the instability of a quantum state, an appropriate metric is essential, yet there is no widely accepted standard. We utilize the operator norm as our quantity of interest and apply graph neural networks to analyze the time evolution of a finite number of atoms in the Jaynes-Cummings model. Our analysis shows that the metrics generated by the graph neural networks effectively capture the instability of the system dynamics. Notably, our approach highlights the importance of the initial conditions, bond connections, and specific operators in evaluating chaos. By interpreting the learned metrics, we demonstrate that the operator norm can be an overly sensitive indicator of chaos, while the linear entropy provides a more balanced perspective. Ultimately, our framework delivers a practical method for measuring the complexity of closed quantum systems, offering a way to explore the intricate dynamics of isolated, non-equilibrium systems. Moreover, we show that the operator norm can be an overly sensitive measure, and recommend using the linear entropy instead. This may seem counterintuitive, as the linear entropy is generally considered a more gentle indicator of chaos. However, our analysis indicates that the dynamics of the Jaynes-Cummings model are complex enough that a more nuanced perspective is necessary. Consider a parameter space divided into subspaces by simple inequalities, represented by vertices in a geometric formation such as a convex shape, and assume that the distribution of the parameter follows a Dirichlet process defined by these vertices. The Dirichlet process estimation framework can be applied to this distribution to find the expected value of a function of the parameter, specifically its average, based on the shape of the geometric formation and the weights of its vertices. However, determining the expected value of a function of the parameter through Dirichlet process estimation requires knowledge of the precision matrix associated with the Dirichlet process, which can be challenging to obtain, especially in cases involving high-dimensional data. In such situations, a generalised maximum likelihood estimation approach can be employed to find the weights that maximise the likelihood of observing the current data, subject to the constraints defined by the geometric formation, resulting in an efficient and computationally simple method for estimating the average of the parameter mixture. This generalised maximum likelihood approach can be applied to various geometric formations, enabling the investigation of various sampling scenarios. Focusing on the specific scenario of a mixture of two parameters separated by a threshold, we derive an explicit expression for the weighted average as the threshold value, which can be used to determine this value from data, thereby providing a method for assessing the number of components in a mixture. This approach is further illustrated through simulations and real-world data analyses, involving microarray and genomic data. The generalised maximum likelihood assessment of the average of parameters of mixtures, coupled with the Dirichlet process estimation framework, has significant implications for the analysis of high-dimensional data, especially in the context of genomic and microarray studies, where prior knowledge is often lacking. The R code for the methods presented in this paper is available from the authors' website. The paper also appears in the journal Biometrics, Vol. 61, No. 3, September 2005, pp. 729-737, under the title "Generalized maximum likelihood assessment of the average of parameters of mixtures, with applications to sampling". Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying principles behind their success remain poorly understood. A growing body of research uses acquisition function to derive benefits from the knowledge possessed by deep learning models, without relying on their interpretability. Despite these advantages, there is a lack of existing code for evaluating and optimizing these knowledge tracing models, despite their widespread use. To address this issue, we present PyKT, a Python-based framework designed to evaluate and optimize deep learning-based knowledge tracing models using acquisition functions. This framework provides multiple evaluation metrics, the ability to plot acquisition functions, and the option to use grid search for optimization. PyKT is tailored to suit the needs of researchers working with knowledge tracing models, and is available for public use at the specified URL.

Given any open set $\Omega$ in $\mathbb{C}^n$, we demonstrate the existence of a linear operator $P$ of elliptic order $m$ with respect to the variable $x$ from the set $\Omega$ with compact support in the variable $t$, such that the span of the set of operators obtained by applying formal Lie derivatives to $P$, when acted upon by the Lie algebra of holomorphic vector fields defined on $\Omega$, is vast and includes the capacity to approximate constants and any differential operator of finite order with respect to the variable $t$ with leading order term independent of $x$ up to a multiplicative constant. In particular, this implies that the set of operators obtained by applying formal Lie derivatives to $P$, when acted upon by the Lie algebra of holomorphic vector fields defined on $\Omega$, has closure equal to the set of operators obtained by applying formal Lie derivatives to the leading order term of $P$. This result extends a previous finding by Bony for the case $\Omega = \mathbb{C}^n$. Additionally, we provide a key lemma regarding the composition of operators obtained by applying formal Lie derivatives to $P$, which may be useful in its own right. Lastly, this result can also be viewed as a variation of a previous finding by Hörmander for the case where $\Omega$ is a compact manifold without boundary. The main innovation of this work is the introduction of a new weight function, which enables the use of a result from Bony's work even in the presence of compactness issues within $\Omega$. This weight function is obtained through the use of a result from a work by Folland, which provides a means of smoothly scaling a support of a given function while maintaining control over the size of the support and the value of the function at a chosen point. This approach can be applied to a broader class of open sets in $\mathbb{C}^n$ than previously known, and it allows for the extension of previously established results to a more general setting. Nevertheless, this work also demonstrates that the span of the set of operators obtained by applying formal Lie derivatives to $P$, when acted upon by the Lie algebra of holomorphic vector fields defined on $\Omega$, is not vast in the sense that it does not include the capacity to approximate differential operators of finite order with respect to the variable $t$ with leading order term dependent on $x$ up to a multiplicative constant, which is a distinct case requiring a separate analysis. Ten years ago, at the inaugural PxTP workshop, fully automated proof production remained a subject of speculation for its potential to revolutionize theorem proving within the scope of SMT solving. Although significant progress has been made since then in developing efficient strategies for proof creation, various challenges remain, including optimizing memory usage and incorporating additional proof techniques effectively. Our proposed solution involves developing a general framework for proof structures that can be applied broadly and is suitable for integrating with diverse SMT solvers and proof-producing strategies. Our proof structure framework, known as Alethe, is composed of a straightforward and extensible core and provides a rich set of attributes to facilitate user-defined extensions. We are presenting an initial incarnation of the Alethe framework in the hopes of stimulating discussion and further collaboration among researchers and developers working on theorem proving and SMT solving. We are particularly interested in exploring ways to enhance strategies for proof production and to integrate our framework with multiple solvers and strategies. If you are a solver developer with an established infrastructure looking to integrate our framework, or a strategy developer seeking a more versatile proof structure, we encourage you to visit the Alethe website at https://alethe.github.io/ to learn more about this project. We welcome your participation and collaboration wholeheartedly. Our discussion on Alethe has been ongoing at the #pxtp channel on Freenode. We look forward to meeting you at the PxTP workshop held in conjunction with the Conference on Automated Reasoning at the University of Cambridge.
